| Notes | | |
| | Matt Olson's 2025 results fell short of his peak power standards, but remained consistent in other areas. For the fourth year in a row, the 32-year-old played in all 162 games and flirted with another 30/100/100 season. His 2026 projections still forecast elite home run totals and strong RBI production, supported by consistent barrel rates and everyday cleanup duties in Atlanta. Olson's 2025 batting average (.272) was buoyed by a .333 BABIP, so expect regression to around the .250 mark this year. His power floor is among the safest at the position. Olson profiles as a reliable early-round source of HR and RBI, particularly valuable in formats that de-emphasize average. Kelly Kirby - FantasyPros | |

item.title: [fantasy.fangraphs.com] Revering and Roasting Starting Pitchers by ADP Tier
item.dc:creator: Vlad Sedler
item.description: The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. Per our Fantasy Player Rater, Skubal ($35.5), Crochet ($32.8) and Skenes ($30.8) finished 1-2-3 among starting pitchers in all roto formats. item.content:encoded:
The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. That season, Tarik Skubal, Paul Skenes, Garrett Crochet and Zack Wheeler were the top four pitchers drafted. Per our Fantasy Player Rater, Skubal ($35.5), Crochet ($32.8) and Skenes ($30.8) finished 1-2-3 among starting pitchers in all roto formats. Wheeler finished 14th ($22.6) despite his season being cut short. As is the case every single year, to varying degrees, there were mid-round arms who produced elite roto seasons (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Max Fried), as well starters such as Nathan Eovaldi, Matthew Boyd, and Trevor Rogers who provided hefty profit a as late-round picks and free agent acquisitions.
As is also the case every season, there were early-round landmines. Cole Ragans, Blake Snell, and Corbin Burnes all missed at least two-thirds of the season due to injuries. Logan Gilbert investors certainly weren’t thrilled about his abbreviated season with only six wins. Nevertheless, dream seasons from the Crème de la crème instilled an illusion of tranquility at the top of the SP pool for 2026 drafts despite the position’s inherent risks and volatile history.
The calm ominously turned to storm on Opening Day. Paul Skenes couldn’t get out of the first inning against the Mets, allowing five earned runs, as droves of social media melodramatics scolded us: “…and that’s why you never draft pitchers early!” Skenes (174 IP – 200 K – 10 W – 3.82 – 1.12) inevitably lost “fantasy god” status as his price dropped a couple of rounds for 2027 drafts. Skubal was a top 10 pitcher with elite ratios, but did not have his usual season of dominance due to missing 5-6 starts. Crochet was an injury landmine and one of many early-round busts.
There were some wins in the second tier (Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale) as well as disappointments (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Ragans again), but what may be most memorable about last season’s starting pitcher pool was that leagues were won without having to invest in early starting pitchers at all. Of course, that only happened to managers who side-stepped the early-round hitter landmines like Aaron Judge, Ronald Acuña Jr., Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Francisco Lindor and Cal Raleigh. The two top producers – Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler – were post-100 ADP picks. Of the 19 starters who earned $14 or more in 12-team leagues, 13 had an ADP of 100+, including six with an ADP of 250 or greater.

A quick review of this group shouldn’t elicit much bewilderment besides maybe Nick Martinez. Most of the other top performers with a post-100 ADP were former prospects with breakout and profit potential. Let’s run through each set of five rounds by 2026 NFBC Online Championship (OC) 12-team ADP to review results in relation to draft price. Expect some takeaways for 2027 drafts along the way. Pitchers who were traded are listed with the team they were on in March.
| Player | Team | ADP | SP Rank | $ Earned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shohei Ohtani | LAD | 1.8 | 22 | $13.5 |
| Tarik Skubal | DET | 6.9 | 8 | $22.8 |
| Paul Skenes | PIT | 9.8 | 30 | $9.9 |
| Garrett Crochet | BOS | 12.0 | 113 | -$7.7 |

SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
These are the pitchers with ADPs in the first five rounds of OCs. Ohtani could technically be excluded since he was mostly used as a hitter in NFBC formats last season. He did earn nearly $14, producing sparkling ratios (1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP) with 95 strikeouts in 85.2 innings (14 starts). Ohtani should pitch again next season, but will be a top-three consensus fantasy pick regardless. No matter where he signs, Skubal will be the first or second SP off draft boards, along with Misiorowski. Sale, Yamamoto and Cristopher Sánchez will likely live in the Round 2 range. Sale was the SP3 in 2024, SP20 in 2025 and SP4 in 2026. Yamamoto was the SP7 and SP3 in his first two full Major League seasons. Sánchez has posted consecutive seasons of 200+ innings and a sub-3.00 ERA. Hunter Brown will be a polarizing pick in the Rounds 4-7 range coming off a 20-start season where he produced a strong 3.19 ERA, but saw his WHIP and walk rate balloon from the previous season — from 1.03 and 7.8% to 1.27 and 12.2%.
A fantasy bust in 2026, Freddy Peralta is quickly surging back up confidence meters and draft boards with his dominant playoff performances. Bryan Woo and Logan Gilbert will be slightly discounted coming off disappointing seasons, but T-Mobile Park in Seattle remains advantageous to starting pitchers (30-of-30 in MLB Park Factor for hits in 2026) and bounce-backs wouldn’t be shocking, assuming good health. Ragans underwent UCL repair surgery in July and has a 10-12 month return timetable, so he’s off our radars for the forseeable future. Jacob deGrom was slightly more human in his age-38 season, posting a career-worst 4.20 ERA, albeit with a 3.11 FIP, 3.14 xFIP and 3.15 SIERA.
Fried’s UCL is “in a good place” according to NY Daily News writer, Gary Phillips. Logan Webb is no longer the position’s Iron Man and could fall out of the top 100 ADP, though he will always have supporters. A healthy Webb could provide profit at a reasonable cost.

SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
The 61-120 ADP range was quite the mixed bag.
Dylan Cease and Jesús Luzardo were studs and will be drafted in the top 50 in most formats.
Wheeler recovered thoroughly from his thoracic outlet procedure and produced yet another $20+ season: 162 IP (28 starts) – 193 K – 14 W – 3.00 – 1.05. He has been the best pitcher in the Majors since 2021, leading in wins (79), ERA (2.92) and second in strikeouts (1,234) behind Cease’s 1,345.
Chase Burns will be highly coveted after his masterful performance over his first full season (154.1 IP – 185 K – 15 W – 2.86 – 1.17) and will be drafted among the top 12 to 15 starters. Nolan McLean will be slightly cheaper than Burns after his first full and successful season in the Majors. Cases made against either this offseason will start with concerns about their lack of elite control and potential WHIP damage at Tier 2 SP prices. Eury Pérez is in this boat as well after posting a 10.3% walk rate and a 1.21 WHIP, though don’t expect to pay anything but a premium for the coveted fireballer who will turn 24 in April.
Joe Ryan should be a solid pick among the top 100 as well. Though he may never have that 180+ IP dream season where good health and all the cards align, Ryan has been a dependable fantasy stud, posting a K-BB% over 20% for four straight seasons and has made between 23 and 30 starts over his first five full seasons.
There were quite a few negative value guys in this range, which was quite shocking for some: George Kirby, Kyle Bradish, Framber Valdez, Kevin Gausman and Emmet Sheehan. Kirby is quickly becoming persona non grata in the fantasy community, posting a painful 1.40 WHIP last season and two straight years with a 4.00+ ERA. Bradish’s WHIP (1.42) was even worse than Kirby’s as he did most of his damage after the All-Star break, posting a 5.29 ERA and a .398 wOBA in those final 10 starts before getting shelved due to lower abdominal pain and being diagnosed with a sports hernia. Gausman compiled 30+ starts for a sixth consecutive season. Despite nearly all of his rate stats and underlying metrics matching last season’s, Gausman posted a 4.51 ERA, with an xFIP and SIERA over a full run lower. I’ll remind myself of how solid everything looked under the hood for Gausman and would consider targeting him again in 2027 drafts. Sheehan isn’t going to fly under the radar this draft season despite last year’s poor results. The key here, of course, is Sheehan having a rotation spot. He dominated in his time down in Triple-A and fired three gems for the Dodgers in September (0.53 ERA, 24:3 K:BB in 17 innings/3 starts).

The 120-180 ADP range was Landmine Central — pitchers like Castillo, Imai, and Chandler decimated our ratios. There were likely some folks who were duped for another round of category destruction when Castillo joined the White Sox. Castillo’s 5.85 ERA was third-worst among the 94 pitchers who threw at least 130 innings. The only ones worse were Kyle Freeland (6.65) and Jeffrey Springs (6.18). At least both of them had bad home parks as an excuse.
Rasmussen and Gray sported matching 2.72 ERAs and finished as top 12 starters. Both will be highly coveted by drafters and I’m sure that the Rasmussen helium will take soar him into the third round of 12-teamers, especially with the glow of playoff glory. Gray dazzled with a below-average strikeout rate of 21.8%, which was 6-7% lower than his two previous seasons in St. Louis. Because of some peripheral drop-offs and his age (36), don’t be surprised to see Gray fall into some offseason bust articles.
Imanaga had three massive disaster starts in the second half of May, but his overall production was strong and his control is on the border of elite. He posted a 5.2% walk rate and a 24.6% strikeout rate and owns a 19.4% K-BB% over three Major League seasons. He’s a free agent who the Cubs would love to re-sign, though we should expect the Padres to show strong interest. I’m definitely interested in Imanaga next season.
Robbie Ray is also a free agent who should generate offseason interest. He will certainly experience a price dip from the 100s to the 200s after a visit from the control boogie man (12% BB) last season.
Gavin Williams led the AL in strikeouts, fueled by an impressive 15% swinging-strike rate. More importantly, he reduced a near-12% walk rate down to below nine percent last season. Williams won’t be cheap in drafts, and rightfully so.

SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
There were some stretches of fantasy usefulness from several in this tier, but no big payoffs. Ryan Weathers’ first season in the AL was a roller coaster ride, but mostly positive. He finished the season with a 3.60 ERA aligned with peripherals (3.50 SIERA, 3.44 xFIP), a 1.22 WHIP, and a 18.5% K-BB%. His roto value was weighed down by just five victories. Carlos Rodón was a properly discounted stash who was activated on May 10 and pitched nine starts before elbow inflammation reappeared and he missed two months of the summer. The end-of-season line was good (2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 26.8% K in 16 starts). His 11.2% walk rate wasn’t and it was his first season over 10% in the post-Covid era. An air of trepidation will likely always remain for Rodón because of his elbow, which may result in a 2027 discount, with profitability a likely outcome if his UCL stays intact.
Jack Flaherty and Zac Gallen are falling semi-stars who were unmitigated disasters last season. Gallen finished with a 3-9 record and a 6.07 ERA in 105.1 innings. Flaherty threw just 88.1 innings and had a 4.48 ERA with his typical high strikeout rate (26%). Flaherty and Gallen are both free agents. They’ll be more appealing to real-life teams than to fantasy managers.
Tanner Bibee makes 30 starts a season, but is essentially just a thrower now. He has posted an ERA over 4.00 for a second straight season and has seen his strikeout rate reduced in three consecutive seasons — from 26.3% to 21.3% to 19%. Bibee has three years left on his 5yr, $45M deal.
Trey Yesavage was certainly trending toward Miz and Schlittler range this winter and early spring, earning a minimum pick of 113 in Online Championships. Yesavage ADP helium was quickly popped a week before Opening Day because of right shoulder impingement. In the Too Early Meatball draft in August, Yesavage was drafted in the 15th round, and this is a 15-team format. It would hard to imagine Yesavage not rising up boards back into the top 150 overall. He has a spot in the Jays rotation so all he needs know is to stay healthy.

SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
A long list of names, so we’ll just touch on a few of them. Among the studs who provided tremendous profit were Cade Cavalli, Reid Detmers, Nick Martinez, Payton Tolle, and the impenetrable Eduardo Rodriguez, who pulled off 17 wins with a 2.89 ERA despite a much higher xFIP (4.44) and SIERA (4.62) and the lowest BABIP (.274 of his career). I don’t usually mess with the peripheral gods and will stubbornly skip over him in early drafts. Cade Cavalli had an epic run after the All-Star break, posting a 90:16 K:BB and a 1.90 ERA over his final 12 starts. Reid Detmers was having a decent season, but really began to shine when the Angels fired pitching coach Mike Maddux. Over those final 8 starts, Detmers posted a 4-0 record with a 1.62 ERA and an impressive 55:5 K:BB. Angels fans are hoping that the new regime under new owner Stan Kroenke will bring the organization from the basement to at least the living room. Interim GM John Mozeliak will stay in the role for now and help the Angels find a permanent GM and a new manager, since Kurt Suzuki is one-and-done.
A $1.20 earning shouldn’t detract from the admiration that Clay Holmes should receive after Round 15 in 12-teamers. He produced a respectable 3.29 ERA, but his low value was impacted by a low strikeout rate (18.6%), six wins, and time spent on the IL, which led to just 18 starts on the season. Michael Wacha was stellar yet again, earning $10 in 12-team NFBC roto leagues as the SP29. Taj Bradley, Troy Melton, Ian Seymour, Justin Wrobleski, and Michael Soroka all had some strong stretches of production that helped fantasy managers, especially those who got out of the Wrobleski business before that ship began to sank. Seymour and Melton are already earning some early 2027 draft love, getting scooped up among the top 50 starters in the 150-175 ADP range — a price that is likely to surge as we move through the heart of draft season.
Finally, a shout out to FAAB stud Sean Burke who broke out in a big way. He produced a 3.34 ERA, a 1.20 WHIP and punched out 185 batters over 172.1 innings. Burke had a scorching-hot nine-start run from June 18 through August 11 where he rocked a 1.60 ERA and struck out 79, with just 11 walks over 62 innings. He had some rough starts, but was still worth every free agent penny. Based on some of the prices (2-5% of budget), it almost felt like pennies were what were being spent.
It’s always a good idea to dig into player stats not long after the season has ended. It helps avoid building biases that may fester, resonate, and solidify within our draft tendencies for the coming draft season. When we wait too long into the winter to review individual player profiles, we increase the likelihood of outside influences manipulating our valuations of players — whether it’s articles that do a good job of convincing a player is a boon or a bust, social media bandwaggoning, or ADP data itself. We don’t have to decide between Ashcraft and McLean now, but if we’re equipped with the details of their stats, underlying metrics, velocity trends, pitch mix changes, Stuff, and healthy history, we can limit emotion and bias from our decision-making and make optimal, objective decisions during the heart of draft season.
Vlad writes for RotoGraphs and is the head of fantasy baseball content at FTN Fantasy. He is a Tout Wars Expert League champ, member of the CDM Fantasy Sports Hall of Fame and has been nominated for FSWA writing awards six times. Vlad has been playing fantasy baseball since 1995, winning 42 NFBC leagues since 2012 and ranking in the top percentile in NFBC’s Online Championship contest (33% win rate, 52% cash rate; 64 leagues). Much to the chagrin of his colleagues and most baseball aficionados, Vlad is a lifelong Dodgers fan who claims his first gut call at age 9 was Kirk Gibson’s 1988 World Series home run. You can follow him on X and BlueSky @RotoGut.

item.content:encoded:
The World Series is about to begin, and we’re being treated to a doozy of a series between the Brewers and the Rays. However, for the 28 other teams, they are turning their attention to 2027, so we’ll join them in that for a bit with some starting pitcher rankings for next season.
This is now my fourth year publishing my starting pitcher rankings and my second year doing it this early. In many ways, I like doing a first pass at rankings this year. At this point, it’s hard to overthink. Most players aren’t playing games or posting videos of new pitches, so there is nothing to get geeked about. Instead, these rankings are more “gut feel” rankings based on how I feel about all of these pitchers at the end of the season. While I tried not to get too in the weeds about stats, I did look back at the general profile that allowed a pitcher to finish among the top 30 overall starters in recent years, and tried to prioritize pitchers who fit that profile, which mostly meant elevating pitchers who get swings and misses, and penalizing pitchers who don’t seem like a good bet for a full season of innings.
As always, the pitchers are split into tiers based on their skillset or what they’ll provide your fantasy team. The tiers themselves are more important than the rankings inside the tiers, so I wouldn’t split hairs over a few spots in the rankings. I’ve also ranked these pitchers as if I’m doing a 12-team league, so safe but boring low-end starters take a hit in value, etc. I won’t have really long write-ups here, but I’ll be back with updated rankings after the new year, where we can get a little more into the nitty-gritty of the rankings.
OK? Ok, so let’s get started.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Starting Pitcher Rankings
| Rank | Player | Team | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| Aces | | | | |
| 1 | Jacob Misiorowski | MIL | No | Aces |
| 2 | Tarik Skubal | Free Agent | No | Aces |
| 3 | Cam Schlittler | NYY | No | Aces |
| 4 | Cristopher Sánchez | PHI | No | Aces |
| 5 | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | LAD | No | Aces |
There’s not much to discuss about these aces. All five posted a K-BB% of at least 21%, and four of them carried a Stuff+ of 113 or higher. They seem like the clear top five starters in baseball, if they can remain healthy.
| Fringe Young Aces | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 6 | Chase Burns | CIN | No | Young power arms |
| 7 | Payton Tolle | BOS | No | Young power arms |
| 8 | Logan Gilbert | SEA | No | Strikeout guys |
| 9 | Paul Skenes | PIT | No - Maybe? | Young power arms |
There’s an argument to be made for all of these guys being aces. Obviously, Paul Skenes is the key name because he was an ace coming into last season and then posted a
3.82 ERA with a 3.34 SIERA. His Stuff+ also fell from 110 in 2025 to 99 this past season, and he didn’t look fully healthy. Still, he’s one year removed from a 1.97 ERA over 187 IP and was the best young arm in baseball. It’s hard to completely ignore 2024 and 2025. All four of these guys finished with a K-BB% between 20% and 22%, and all are power-first pitchers. Chase Burns threw 154.1 IP with a 2.86 ERA, 3.46 SIERA, 14.4% SwStr%, and 112 Stuff+, and I think that innings number will rise, which will give him even more value. Payton Tolle’s first full season was 148.2 IP with a 3.03 ERA, 21.7% K-BB, and 115 Stuff+. Like Burns, I also expect his innings to rise and his value to tick up.
| Aces With Injury Risk | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 10 | Chris Sale | ATL | No (Previous risk) | Elite vets, health risk |
| 11 | Garrett Crochet | BOS | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
| 12 | Jacob deGrom | TEX | No (Previous risk) | Elite vets, health risk |
| 13 | Zack Wheeler | PHI | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
| 14 | Bryan Woo | SEA | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 15 | Jesús Luzardo | PHI | No | Elite vets, health risk |
| 16 | Dylan Cease | TOR | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
If you wanted to take any of these starters over the guys in the tier above, that wouldn’t be crazy. They’re not down in this tier because they’re worse pitchers; they’re in this tier because they carry more injury risk than the pitchers in the tier above, and injury risk with your ace is a serious gamble. Chris Sale and Jacob deGrom have been healthy the last two years, but have a lengthy injury history, while Garrett Crochet missed essentially the entire year with an injury, and Dylan Cease saw his velocity plummet at the end of the season and then ended the year on the IL with a shoulder injury. You draft this group for ace outcomes at a price that already reflects the innings risk.
| Ace Upside - Limited Track Record | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 17 | Drew Rasmussen | TBR | No (Previous Risk) | WHIP guys |
| 18 | Cade Cavalli | WSN | Coming off injury | Rising arms, unproven |
| 19 | Braxton Ashcraft | PIT | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 20 | Logan Henderson | MIL | Coming off injury | Rising arms, unproven |
| 21 | Gavin Williams | CLE | No | Rising arms, unproven |
Almost everyone here has one strong season to point to, which is why the tier name fits. Of course, Drew Rasmussen has more than one good season, but he also has had three elbow surgeries and has only pitched over 150 innings once in his MLB career. That prevents me from drafting him where I think his talent should have him because he carries so much extra risk. Cade Cavalli and Logan Henderson also have injury track records that make me a little bit concerned about their durability, and Cavalli’s breakout 2026 season was so closely tied to a velocity increase that I’m just not sure if I want to fully ignore the first three months of the season for him, which were pretty inconsistent. This feels like a fair hedge on the bets for Cavalli. Gavin Williams arguably has the best skills of the group (2.95 SIERA, 25.1% K-BB, 15% SwStr%), but he also had a 3.76 ERA because he is prone to losing his command for an inning in basically every outing.
| High-End SP2 Without Elite K% | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 22 | Parker Messick | CLE | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 23 | Max Fried | NYY | Yes | Weak contact and durability |
| 24 | Griffin Jax | TBR | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 25 | Hunter Brown | HOU | Yes | Weak contact and durability |
These four are valuable because of ERA and WHIP, not big strikeout totals. Parker Messick had moments where he looked like a fantasy ace, but he has just a 97 Stuff+ and his strikeout rate is not the same as the guys in the tier above. Max Fried had another solid season, but his fantasy finishes over the last four years have been super inconsistent because he seems to always miss time with an injury. Hunter Brown was clearly hurt and not pitching well this season, but his strikeout numbers also fell off a cliff in the second half of last season, so I’m not sure we can really rely on him for strikeouts. Griffin Jax is an interesting bet because he only moved into the rotation in the middle of the season, but he had 103.1 innings as a starter and registered a 3.14 ERA, 18.8% K-BB, and 13.6% SwStr%. That’s pretty damn good.
| There’s an Ace in There Somewhere | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 26 | Joe Ryan | MIN | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 27 | Jared Jones | PIT | Yes | Rising arms, unproven |
| 28 | Reid Detmers | LAA | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 29 | Blake Snell | LAD | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 30 | Shohei Ohtani | LAD | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 31 | Carlos Rodón | NYY | Yes | Power arms, command concern |
| 32 | Nolan McLean | NYM | No | Young power arms |
| 33 | Eury Pérez | MIA | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 34 | Emmet Sheehan | LAD | No | Rising arms, unproven |
This tier is a bet on ceiling, and the group has the skills to justify it, but not the track record of consistent production. Obviously, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani, and Carlos Rodon are all in here because of injury concerns that prevent me from giving them enough innings to have them qualify as an ace. Reid Detmers finally had his breakout year in 185.0 innings with a 3.36 ERA and 22.0% K-BB, and Jared Jones shook the rust after his return from injury and pitched 101.2 innings with a 3.28 SIERA and 22.2% K-BB. He really came on at the end of the season. We also still see enough strikeout upside and raw, natural ability from Nolan McLean, Eury Perez, and Emmet Sheehan to have them here. I do worry that McLean had just a 9.6% swinging strike rate, and there may not be as much strikeout upside as people want to believe. This is the range that Misiorowski and Schlittler were going last year, and somebody in here is going to make that jump.
| No Longer Aces, But Safe Floor | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 35 | Gerrit Cole | NYY | No | Strikeout guys |
| 36 | Sonny Gray | BOS | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 37 | Shota Imanaga | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 38 | Logan Webb | SFG | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 39 | Freddy Peralta | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 40 | Sandy Alcantara | MIA | No | Weak contact and durability |
The pitchers here have a long record of quality, and the case for them is volume and ratios. Sandy Alcantara is probably the weakest of the bunch, but he threw 211 innings this season, and we’re back to getting that bulk production from him; a 4.24 SIERA is just not ideal. Freddy Peralta has turned his season around with the Rays, and we’ve seen him be a good starting pitcher for too long to not assume he can continue to pitch well in 2027.
| Fun Upside With Volatility | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 41 | Ian Seymour | TBR | No | Strikeout guys |
| 42 | Andrew Painter | PHI | No | Strikeout guys |
| 43 | Christian Scott | NYM | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 44 | Kade Anderson | SEA | No | Top prospects, clear 2027 job |
| 45 | Kaima Taira | Intl (NPB) | No | International, unproven |
| 46 | Walbert Ureña | LAA | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
The appeal here is strikeout ability, and the risk is large, which is why they’re all down in this range. Ian Seymour flashed the best MLB skills in the tier. In 77 innings as a starter this season, he posted a 2.84 SIERA, 26.7% K-BB, and 14.4% SwStr%. I know the 4.44 ERA wasn’t tremendous, but I believe in the underlying skill set here. Andrew Painter made some key pitch mix changes in the second half of the season that I really like, but, much like Cavalli, his ability to hold velocity will be crucial. Walbert Ureña is confusing. He throws hard and has a nasty changeup plus a sweeper that flashed the ability to miss bats this season. You watch him pitch, and you see a potential stud. But his four-seamer is pretty average, and his 4.14 SIERA and 12.3% K-BB% say he got lucky this season.
The two biggest wild cards here are Kade Anderson and Kaima Taira. Anderson was the top pitching prospect in baseball, but he relies on command and movement over velocity and raw stuff, so it remains to be seen how that translates at the big league level. Taira is almost certain to come over from Japan this offseason after pitching to a 1.36 ERA and 0.97 WHIP with 134 K and 44 BB over 139 IP in NPB this year. We’ve heard he touches 100 mph, has an eight-pitch mix, and could be the best pitching free agent this offseason, other than Skubal.
| Boring But It Can Work | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 47 | Kevin Gausman | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 48 | Aaron Nola | PHI | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 49 | George Kirby | SEA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
All of these guys had pretty gross ERAs but underlying metrics that say they pitched better than the results. We just have to decide if we believe that or not. Aaron Nola made some pitch mix changes in the second half (limiting elevated fastballs) that helped him to produce better results, but George Kirby simply never got it going this year. The draft case for each of these guys is innings, a discounted price based on ERA over SIERA, and a decent chance of a bounce-back, with Kevin Gausman the safest of the three, depending on where he signs.
| Hurt But Should Be Healthy Opening Day | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 50 | Nathan Eovaldi | Free Agent | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 51 | Shane McClanahan | TBR | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 52 | Max Meyer | MIA | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 53 | Ryan Weathers | NYY | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 54 | Ryan Pepiot | TBR | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 55 | Pablo López | MIN | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
| 56 | Nick Pivetta | SDP | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 57 | Corbin Burnes | ARI | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
| 58 | Tyler Glasnow | LAD | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
This is another tier of injuries. These guys ended the season hurt or were hurt for basically the entire year. However, all of them seem likely to begin the year healthy and on the mound for their respective teams. You’re drafting them if the injury discount leaves a bigger gap than the missed time justifies.
| Is There a Next Step? | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 59 | Jackson Jobe | DET | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 60 | Didier Fuentes | ATL | No | Strikeout guys |
| 61 | Trey Yesavage | TOR | Yes | Power arms, command concern |
| 62 | Roki Sasaki | LAD | No | Young power arms |
| 63 | Taj Bradley | MIN | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 64 | Sean Burke | CHW | No | Strikeout guys |
| 65 | Nick Lodolo | CIN | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 66 | River Ryan | DET | Yes | Top prospects, clear 2027 job |
These pitchers have flashed the physical tools, but the consistent results are not there yet. Roki Sasaki, Taj Bradley, and Sean Burke all had stretches in 2026 where they showed clear improvement from 2025. But those stretches didn’t last. Can we count of them in 2027? Trey Yesavage and Jackson Jobe both spent most of the year recovering from injury, but they are top pitching prospects who have shown upside when on the mound. Didier Fuentes was lights out in relief for Atlanta and should get a chance to start, and River Ryan figures to be in the rotation for the Tigers after being the headliner in the Skubal deal. He has flashed real ability before, but he needs to stay healthy.
| More About Command or Weak Contact | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 67 | Trevor Rogers | Free Agent | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 68 | Troy Melton | DET | No | WHIP guys |
| 69 | Sean Manaea | NYM | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 70 | Michael King | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 71 | Framber Valdez | DET | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 72 | Foster Griffin | Free Agent | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 73 | Emerson Hancock | SEA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 74 | Jake Bennett | BOS | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 75 | Tyler Mahle | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 76 | Ranger Suarez | BOS | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 77 | Michael Wacha | KCR | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
These pitchers win with walks and contact, not strikeouts, and many have a Stuff+ under 100 (Tyler Mahle 88, Jake Bennett 93, Ranger Suarez 94, Michael King 95). Some of these guys have been top 30 pitchers before and potentially could again, but the ceiling just doesn’t feel overly high. I would draft this group for innings and WHIP, especially in deeper formats.
| Inconsistent But Has Flashed | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 78 | Robert Gasser | MIL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 78 | MacKenzie Gore | TEX | No | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 79 | José Soriano | TOR | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 80 | Joey Cantillo | CLE | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 81 | Will Warren | NYY | No | Young power arms |
| 82 | Tanner Bibee | CLE | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 83 | Connelly Early | WAS | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 84 | Bryce Miller | SEA | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 85 | Andrew Abbott | CIN | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
Every pitcher here has had a good stretch, but none has strung together a full good year. Some of that is due to injury (Bryce Miller and Connelly Early), but there is just a lot of volatility in this group. Even pitchers that have had good full seasons, like Andrew Abbott, have seemingly never had the profile to back up that success. I do like guys like Early, Miller, Joey Cantillo, or MacKenzie Gore as late-round flyers just in case they can ever put it together or stay healthy.
| Could be a Stud, Could be Demoted | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 87 | Ryan Sloan | SEA | No | Depth prospects, unproven |
| 88 | Hagen Smith | CHW | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 89 | Brandon Sproat | MIL | No | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 90 | Connor Prielipp | MIN | No | Strikeout guys |
| 91 | Shane Drohan | MIL | No | Strikeout guys |
| 92 | Reese Olson | DET | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 93 | Jack Leiter | TEX | Yes | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 94 | Zebby Matthews | MIN | No | Strikeout guys |
This tier is about uncertainty, and it mixes prospects with young arms who have not settled in. Hagen Smith may be the most interesting. He made his MLB debut as a reliever with a 1.32 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 37.4% K, 23.4% K-BB, 2.97 SIERA, 14.6% SwStr%, and 108 Stuff+ over 27.1 IP. However, his Triple-A stats were not as good, and he has some major command concerns. Treat this tier as late-round upside.
| Low Upside But a Safe Floor | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 95 | Shane Baz | BAL | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 96 | Merrill Kelly | ARI | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 97 | Matthew Boyd | CHC | No | WHIP guys |
| 98 | Kyle Leahy | STL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 99 | Michael Soroka | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 100 | Noah Cameron | KCR | No | WHIP guys |
| 101 | Peter Lambert | HOU | No | Strikeout guys |
| 102 | Justin Wrobleski | LAD | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 103 | Brandon Pfaadt | ARI | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 104 | Dean Kremer | MIN | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 105 | Ryne Nelson | ARI | No | Strikeout guys |
| 106 | Cody Bradford | TEX | No | WHIP guys |
| 107 | Casey Mize | Free Agent | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 108 | Andre Pallante | STL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
Most of these pitchers will not win you a league, but they are likely to produce solid ratios and good innings totals. Most of these guys feel like streamers or solid targets in 15-team leagues and draft-and-hold formats.
| No Idea What You Are | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 109 | Luis Castillo | CHW | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 110 | Dustin May | Free Agent | No | Strikeout guys |
| 111 | Anthony Kay | CHW | No | Young power arms |
| 112 | Tatsuya Imai | HOU | No | Strikeout guys |
| 113 | Landen Roupp | SFG | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 114 | Matthew Liberatore | STL | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 115 | Jacob Lopez | ATH | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 116 | Janson Junk | MIA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 117 | Brayan Bello | BOS | No | Weak contact and durability |
I think the title of this group kind of says it all. I have no idea what to make of most of these guys. Matthew Liberatore had an intriguing stretch in the second half. Janson Junk has a deep pitch mix and a solid Stuff+ grade. Brayan Bello looked like an entirely different pitcher when he moved into the bulk reliever role. I was high on Landen Roupp for much of last year, but the results never came. Maybe we need to see something in spring from this group, or maybe we avoid.
| Are You Healthy? I’m Interested If Yes | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 118 | Kyle Harrison | MIL | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 119 | Justin Steele | CHC | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 120 | Cade Horton | CHC | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 121 | Kris Bubic | Free Agent | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 122 | Edward Cabrera | CHC | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 123 | Jack Flaherty | Free Agent | Yes | Flagged, but pitched in 2026 |
| 124 | Clarke Schmidt | NYY | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 125 | Luis Gil | NYY | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 126 | Tylor Megill | NYM | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 127 | AJ Smith-Shawver | ATL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
All ten of these arms have an injury discount, and the question heading into your fantasy drafts is whether the production will be there when they return. As of now, I can’t draft any of them as more than a late-round dart throw.
| Young Arms But Might Have Rotation Spots | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 128 | Gage Jump | ATH | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 129 | Quinn Mathews | STL | No | Unclassified |
| 130 | David Sandlin | CHW | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 131 | Jonah Tong | NYM | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 132 | George Klassen | LAA | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 133 | Zac Thornton | NYM | No | WHIP guys |
| 134 | Drew Thorpe | CHW | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 135 | Noah Schultz | CHW | No | Young power arms |
| 136 | Blade Tidwell | SFG | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 137 | J.T. Ginn | ATH | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
Maybe I’m too low on these arms, but I don’t see a lot of security in any of them. All of them have a legit case to be in their team’s starting rotation, but I also see a world where they begin the year in Triple-A. Gage Jump and J.T. Ginn also get dinged for their brutal home park.
| Probably Not Healthy to Begin | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 138 | Spencer Schwellenbach | ATL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 139 | Cole Ragans | KCR | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 140 | Hunter Greene | CIN | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 141 | David Festa | MIN | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 142 | DJ Herz | WSN | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 143 | Nestor Cortes | Free Agent | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 144 | Reynaldo López | ATL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 145 | Bowden Francis | TOR | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 146 | Hurston Waldrep | ATL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 147 | Ben Brown | CHC | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 148 | Brandon Walter | HOU | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 149 | Zach Eflin | BAL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 150 | Jordan Montgomery | Free Agent | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
We end with a tier of guys who we feel confident either won’t begin the year healthy or have missed so much time that it’s hard to know what to get from them. I wanted to list them here because the offseason could change how we rank them, but these are not really names to be targeting in your drafts.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 MLB Postseason is entering the Championship Series, but the time for fantasy baseball analysis never truly stops. Last Monday, we started our Rotoworld Staff and Friends Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft for the 2027 season. While many places do a “too early” mock draft, we’d argue that it’s not really too early to look ahead to next season. I’ve been posting a collection of “look back” articles reviewing the best picks of the 2026 season, the worst picks, and my key lessons, but all of these articles are linked together by the idea that immediately taking stock in the season, before the offseason hype starts to creep in, can be an incredibly valuable experience.
So we invited our staff and a few of our friends to put together a 15-round mock draft that we’ll complete over the next couple of weeks and continue to break down for you in chunks over on our site. Today you’ll get the first four rounds, and then I’ll be back to update the next four or five rounds by the end of the week and then do one more update at the end.
We hope you find it a useful tool, and we’ll see how much it changes over the next few weeks.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft
| Round 1 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 1 | RotoPat (Rotoworld) | Shohei Ohtani | UT/SP | LAD |
| 2 | George Bissell (Rotoworld) | Pete Crow-Armstrong | OF | CHC |
| 3 | Frank Stampfl (CBS Sports) | Bobby Witt Jr. | SS | KC |
| 4 | D.J. Short (Rotoworld) | Elly De La Cruz | SS | CIN |
| 5 | Scott Pianowski (Yahoo Sports) | Fernando Tatis Jr. | 2B/OF | SD |
| 6 | Rivers McCown (Rotoworld) | Junior Caminero | 3B | TB |
| 7 | Matthew Pouliot (Rotoworld) | Aaron Judge | OF | NYY |
| 8 | Dave Shovein (Rotoworld) | Juan Soto | OF | NYM |
| 9 | Frank Ammirante (RotoBaller) | Jackson Chourio | OF | MIL |
| 10 | James Schiano (Rotoworld) | James Wood | OF | WSH |
| 11 | Justin Mason (FanGraphs) | Yordan Alvarez | OF | HOU |
| 12 | Jorge Montanez (Rotoworld) | Ben Rice | 1B | NYY |
Perhaps the story here is that no starting pitchers went in the first 12 picks. One season after Tarik Skubal, Garrett Crochet, and Paul Skenes either got hurt or had down seasons, none of the drafters seemed willing to roll the dice on a starting pitcher with their first pick. Honestly, I can’t blame them. Early-round hitters, on average, continue to out-produce early-round pitchers at similar draft costs. The pitchers that do hit can make a huge difference for your team, but the risk is exponentially higher. A hitter taken here who fails to produce value, like Kyle Tucker this year, can still produce $10 of value, but a pitcher who goes in the first round and fails to produce value is almost always due to injury, and they can give you no value.
We did see Pat still choose Shohei Ohtani (dual position eligible here) as the top pick over Pete Crow-Armstrong. There are certainly some questions as to whether or not Ohtani’s body can hold up to a whole season as a starting pitcher and a DH, which will bring some uncertainty to his fantasy value. We also know he’s clearly not healthy right now, so we’ll need to see if any of these injuries require offseason surgery, but PCA has certainly worked his way into the conversation to be first overall.
A big surprise for some might be seeing Fernando Tatis Jr. this high. The Padres outfielder was one of the best hitters in baseball from June 1st on after a batting stance change allowed him to clear his hips more easily and unlock the pull-side power that we know he has. He also picked up 2B eligibility this season, which will be huge for him at a pretty barren position.
Jackson Chourio and James Wood have used breakout seasons to propel them into the first-round conversation, and you have to wonder if there is yet another level of development there, and Yordan Alvarez now has outfield eligibility in all formats, which makes him an even safer pick here. There look to be plenty of outfield options in the first round, including injured New York stars Juan Soto and Aaron Judge. Both of them being in the first round makes sense, but we may start to have to ask real questions about Judge’s durability. He’ll be 35 years old next season. He’s a giant human being, and the strain of playing the outfield every day at that size takes a real toll on your body. The fact that his two major injuries this season were both soft tissue or muscle injuries (and not a broken toe) should begin to raise some questions about whether or not we can count on 150+ games from Judge going forward.
His teammate, Ben Rice, used a 40-home run season to catapult him into the first round as well. That’s without catcher eligibility. Rice was the first 1B off the board in this draft, and I really find it hard to argue against that. Some guys in the next round have an argument, but Rice is a tremendous overall hitter. He has clear power. He plays in a great park for his approach, and there is no way the Yankees are going back to regularly sitting him against lefties. Even if Rice is more of a mid-30s home run hitter going forward than a true 40+ guy, his approach at the plate makes me feel good about his contact and batting average, and that puts him ahead of the guys who will follow him in round two.
| Round 2 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 13 | Jorge Montanez | CJ Abrams | SS/2B | WSH |
| 14 | Justin Mason | Jose Ramirez | 3B | CLE |
| 15 | James Schiano | Jacob Misiorowski | SP | MIL |
| 16 | Frank Ammirante | Tarik Skubal | SP | LAD |
| 17 | Dave Shovein | Ronald Acuña Jr. | OF | ATL |
| 18 | Matthew Pouliot | Nick Kurtz | 1B | OAK |
| 19 | Rivers McCown | Jordan Walker | OF | STL |
| 20 | Scott Pianowski | Kyle Schwarber | DH | PHI |
| 21 | D.J. Short | Pete Alonso | 1B | BAL |
| 22 | Frank Stampfl | Corbin Carroll | OF | ARI |
| 23 | George Bissell | Cam Schlittler | SP | NYY |
| 24 | Roto Pat | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | SP | LAD |
And now the pitchers start to come off the board. Not really a surprise with who the first three arms were off the board: Jacob Misiorowski, Tarik Skubal, and Cam Schlittler. I assume those will be the top three arms in pretty much all rankings heading into 2027. Pat did snag Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the fourth starter picked in this round, and while some may argue for Chris Sale or Cristopher Sanchez here, there’s a strong case that Yamamoto could be locked into the fourth spot. There is still some elevated risk with starting pitchers in the second round, but at least every one of these teams added an elite bat in the first round, and both George and Pat were able to take second elite bats at the start of the third round, so this risk feels more palatable.
CJ Abrams is another player, like Tatis Jr., who picked up second base eligibility in most formats. That’s huge for his fantasy value. So is hitting .261 with 33 home runs and 34 steals while driving in 106 runs. Abrams will be 26 years old next season, and while his future in Washington is a bit cloudy, he’s an elite offensive talent who is finally making good on that promise.
We had some former first-round picks fall into the second with Jose Ramirez, Ronald Acuña Jr., and Corbin Carroll all falling into the second round. The falls make sense too. Ramirez and Acuña Jr. now just have a bit more injury risk than some of the other players going in the first round. Ramirez still has great upside at a position that lacks talent, which may drive his price up, but he’ll be 34 years old, and he hit just 12 home runs and batted .235 this year after hamate surgery. Are you willing to bet that he gets back to 100% of his old self, or do we think it’s more likely that he’ll be 75-80% of the guy who almost went 40/40 in 2024? Acuña Jr. is a harder bet because he has now played under 108 games in three straight seasons and has played over 120 games once since 2019. It’s hard to bet on a full season of production, and with PCA, Chourio, and James Wood emerging, it makes sense to go with the younger/healthier players.
At the same position, the most interesting name in this round is probably Jordan Walker. He had a breakout season this year, hitting .269 with 29 home runs, 102 RBI, and 22 steals. He also just turned 24 years old, so there is plenty of growth still possible for him. He struggled through an injury at the end of the year, which hurt his September stats, but there will be no half measures with Walker in 2027. You have to either be all-in on the fact that 2026 was a real breakout for a former top prospect or just acknowledge that you won’t be getting him in your drafts.
Pete Alonso and Nick Kurtz are the two first basemen I alluded to earlier who land here in round 2. Kurtz played just 99 games this season due to injury but still hit 21 home runs while batting .256. We know the hitting environment in Sacramento is elite, so he should still be going in this range.
| Round 3 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 25 | Roto Pat | Sal Stewart | 1B | CIN |
| 26 | George Bissell | Konnor Griffin | SS | PIT |
| 27 | Frank Stampfl | Miguel Vargas | 3B | CHW |
| 28 | D.J. Short | Cristopher Sanchez | SP | PHI |
| 29 | Scott Pianowski | Paul Skenes | SP | PIT |
| 30 | Rivers McCown | Mason Miller | RP | SD |
| 31 | Matthew Pouliot | Julio Rodriguez | OF | SEA |
| 32 | Dave Shovein | Trea Turner | SS | PHI |
| 33 | Frank Ammirante | Gunnar Henderson | SS | BAL |
| 34 | James Schiano | Jackson Merrill | OF | SD |
| 35 | Justin Mason | Kevin McGonigle | SS/3B | DET |
| 36 | Jorge Montanez | Jesus Luzardo | SP | PHI |
We see three current-year rookies go in Round 3, announcing themselves as top-tier talents for years to come, and it’s hard to argue against it. Sal Stewart, Konnor Griffin, and Kevin McGonigle all showed that they can handle this level of competition, and we should expect more growth from these young players. The same goes for Miguel Vargas, who is not a rookie but broke out in 2026 in a way that suggests consistent value. He’s always had an elite plate approach, and now he added pull-side power to that equation. Vargas will be 27 years old and is in an ascending lineup, so he belongs in this range.
We saw the next group of starting pitchers go with Cristopher Sanchez, Paul Skenes, and Jesus Luzardo. Obviously, the name everybody will want to talk about is Skenes. It was a bad year for the Pirates ace, and while he claimed he wasn’t hurt, his velocity fell throughout the year, and he was not missing as many bats. There had been some previous concerns that his fastball wasn’t a huge whiff pitch to righties (10.7% swinging strike rate in 2025), but Skenes saw huge strides there this season. However, that was basically the only place he got better, and by elevating his four-seamer more for whiffs, he also started to allow more hard contact. It’s hard to see Skenes being this bad again, but we also can’t ignore how this season went.
Mason Miller went here as the first closer off the board, and three former first-round picks fell in Gunnar Henderson, Trea Turner, and Julio Rodriguez. I covered Gunnar and Trea in my article on what I learned from the 2026 fantasy baseball season, so you should read that, but essentially their 2025 price baked in a full return to peak value and ignored the warning signs from that season. We don’t appear to be doing that this year.
| Round 4 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 37 | Jorge Montanez | Drew Rasmussen | SP | TB |
| 38 | Justin Mason | Chris Sale | SP | ATL |
| 39 | James Schiano | Francisco Lindor | SS | NYM |
| 40 | Frank Ammirante | Kyle Tucker | OF | LAD |
| 41 | Dave Shovein | Brice Turang | 2B | MIL |
| 42 | Matthew Pouliot | Zach Neto | SS | LAA |
| 43 | Rivers McCown | Oneil Cruz | OF | PIT |
| 44 | Scott Pianowski | Matt Olson | 1B | ATL |
| 45 | D.J. Short | Carson Benge | OF | NYM |
| 46 | Frank Stampfl | Chase Burns | SP | CIN |
| 47 | George Bissell | Hunter Goodman | C | COL |
| 48 | Roto Pat | Nolan McLean | SP | NYM |
Now we answer the question of how far Kyle Tucker falls as Frank Ammirante takes him with the fourth pick in the fourth round, 40th overall. I covered Tucker more extensively in my article revisiting the top two rounds of 2025 drafts, but the miss on Tucker was essentially looking at pedigree (his seasons before his last two injured ones) and also the team context (a move to the Dodgers) and ignoring that he hadn’t had a fully productive year in a while. I’m not sure anybody expected that Tucker would see his barrel-rate collapse and that he would make uncharacteristically aggressive, out-of-character swing decisions, so perhaps we can expect a slight bounce back to his previously healthy form.
Four more starting pitchers go off the board here, and it’s an interesting group. Drew Rasmussen was brilliant this season, but it was also his first over 150 innings, and he’s had three elbow surgeries. Can you bank on his health as your ace? Kind of the same question for Chris Sale, who will be 38 next year and has basically alternated healthy years with injured years. After being hurt for basically all of 2021-23, he threw 178 innings in 2024, then 125 in 2025, and then 163 this year. What’s in store for 2027?
The final two arms were young pitchers in Chase Burns and Nolan McLean. The Burns pick makes sense given his elite strikeout upside and plus raw stuff, but McLean is harder to see here. Not that he’s a bad pitcher, but taking him as the 11th starting pitcher is assuming tons of growth. His 26% strikeout rate and 16.6% K-BB% don’t line up with some of the elite arms in this range, and his 10.5% swinging strike rate continues to suggest some concern with his ability to consistently miss bats. He’ll be 26 next year, and he’s clearly a talented arm, but taking him this high means he really HAS to take the next step, or he won’t return value.
Oneil Cruz’s bounce-back season pushed him up into the fourth round, and he’s joined by young outfielder Carson Benge, who hit .282 with 20 home runs and 22 steals in his rookie season. He didn’t get the fanfare of the other rookies who went higher in this draft, but Benge has a true five-category skill set and should be in an improved lineup next season.
We also saw our first catcher go off the board in Hunter Goodman. Keep in mind that this is a one-catcher format, which is why you’re not seeing a lot of catchers go early, but George wanted to lock up an elite bat at the position. With Ben Rice no longer catcher eligible, Goodman was the top fantasy catcher this season after hitting 41 home runs, driving in 88 runs, and hitting .245 in Coors Field. There’s little reason to believe he can’t do it again.
| Round 5 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 49 | Roto Pat | Rafael Devers | 1B | SF |
| 50 | George Bissell | Cade Smith | RP | CLE |
| 51 | Frank Stampfl | Zack Wheeler | SP | PHI |
| 52 | D.J. Short | Parker Messick | SP | CLE |
| 53 | Scott Pianowski | Randy Arozarena | OF | SEA |
| 54 | Rivers McCown | Dylan Cease | SP | TOR |
| 55 | Matthew Pouliot | Vladimir Guerrero Jr. | 1B | TOR |
| 56 | Dave Shovein | Logan Gilbert | SP | SEA |
| 57 | Frank Ammirante | Garrett Crochet | SP | BOS |
| 58 | James Schiano | Bryce Harper | 1B/OF | PHI |
| 59 | Justin Mason | Logan Henderson | SP | MIL |
| 60 | Jorge Montanez | Michael Harris II | OF | ATL |
A few big-name starting pitchers with major injuries go in this round. Zack Wheeler (SP12) missed half of this past season after having thoracic outlet surgery, Garrett Crochet (SP16) missed basically the whole season with a shoulder injury, Dylan Cease (SP14) ended the season on the injured list with a shoulder injury, and Logan Henderson (SP17) has missed time in each of the last two seasons with injuries. We’re now outside of the top 10 starting pitchers, so these guys don’t HAVE to be your ace, but this is still an early round draft pick for pitchers who have some overall health concerns. I understand the argument for their upside, and while I may not make the pick here, that’s just my personal drafting philosophy.
Parker Messick (SP13) and Logan Gilbert (SP15) also go in this round. Both of them feel a bit safer from a health standpoint, and there is still an argument that Gilbert has another level of production to hit. I have him as a top-10 starting pitcher, so I like him going as the 15th starter off the board.
We see Cade Smith go here as the second closer off the board, and Rafael Devers and Bryce Harper make sense in this range as veteran 1B who are likely past their peak but continue to produce overall solid numbers. Devers really turned things around after a slow start to the year and seems as consistent as ever.
We also see two outfielders coming off big seasons in Michael Harris II and Randy Arozarena. James Schiano and I actually discussed this exact either-or in a video we recorded after the Braves were eliminated from the postseason. I picked Harris II easily because I believe in the changes he’s made over the last year-and-a-half, and I’m not looking to pay for Arozarena’s career year.
Lastly, we need to address Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who finally goes off the board here in the fifth. We all know how Vlad Jr. struggled this year, but he’s now going as the sixth 1B, late in the fifth round, which is way more palatable for me. I know the power wasn’t there, but we have enough of a track record to feel confident that he is at least a 20-25 home run bat who can hit .280 in what should be a solid lineup. That’s still a solid fantasy asset; it’s just not a pick to make in the first three rounds of your draft. Also, getting corrective eye surgery can’t be bad either.
| Round 6 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 61 | Jorge Montanez | Jac Caglianone | OF | KC |
| 62 | Justin Mason | Jhoan Duran | RP | PHI |
| 63 | James Schiano | Jazz Chisholm Jr. | OF | NYY |
| 64 | Frank Ammirante | Cal Raleigh | C | SEA |
| 65 | Dave Shovein | Andres Munoz | RP | SEA |
| 66 | Matthew Pouliot | Bryan Woo | SP | SEA |
| 67 | Rivers McCown | Drake Baldwin | C | ATL |
| 68 | Scott Pianowski | Alex Bregman | 3B | CHC |
| 69 | D.J. Short | Gavin Williams | SP | CLE |
| 70 | Frank Stampfl | Shea Langeliers | C | OAK |
| 71 | George Bissell | Kade Anderson | SP | SEA |
| 72 | Roto Pat | Wyatt Langford | OF | TEX |
This is a super interesting round to me, and I can’t make much sense of it, haha. There seem to be no runs here or any real trend.
We do get more catchers off the board here with Cal Raleigh, Drake Baldwin, and Shea Langeliers. It feels a little early to be in a one-catcher format, but everybody has their own strategy. Baldwin feels like a great pick after his 2026 season, and while I do think Raleigh is going to bounce back after a down 2026 season, I’m not sure he’d be the gamble I take this early in the sixth round. Yes, you might be getting 30+ home runs from that spot, but the batting average will be a drain, and we have no idea if that lineup will be any good.
Jhoan Duran goes off the board as the third closer, and then Andres Munoz next was a bit of a surprise. He wasn’t really in a closer committee in Seattle this year; they just didn’t get a lot of saves. His SIERA and underlying metrics look a lot better than his ERA, so it does feel like he was just unlucky, but I’m not that convinced the Mariners will be that good next year, and Munoz has never delivered as a consistent top 5-8 closer.
Three risky hitters with plenty of upside also go in this round: Jac Caglianone, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Wyatt Langford. We don’t really know where Jazz will be next year, but it seems like it won’t be New York. That’s likely a big park downgrade for him. His batting average also regressed pretty drastically this season, which had been a concern for him in previous years. We know the speed will always be there, so he’ll need to land in a park where the power can come as well, but this feels like a fair spot for him. Caglianone is also a popular breakout pick because his batted ball data has been really strong. I like the idea of him taking a big step next season, but a top-60 pick does feel like you’re paying as if the breakthrough is a given. We all know the deal with Langford at this point too. A top-70 pick on him feels right if he can stay healthy, but can he ever stay healthy?
Bryan Woo at SP18 and Gavin Williams at SP19 feel like strong picks at this point. Both of them have immense strikeout upside and the ability to be top-10 starting pitchers. Woo had a bad stretch this season but seemed to right the ship at the end of the year, and Williams still seems to have one iffy inning every game where his command gets wonky. However, the big surprise here was Kade Anderson. I know he was an elite pitching prospect, but he doesn’t have elite MLB velocity or Stuff+, which means that he gets by with command and a deep enough pitch mix. I think he will be a solid starting pitcher, but I’m not sure I see the ceiling to take him as SP20, especially in what will be his rookie season.
| Round 7 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 73 | Roto Pat | Henry Bolte | OF | OAK |
| 74 | George Bissell | Riley Greene | OF | DET |
| 75 | Frank Stampfl | Andy Pages | OF | LAD |
| 76 | D.J. Short | William Contreras | C | MIL |
| 77 | Scott Pianowski | Ceddanne Rafaela | OF | BOS |
| 78 | Rivers McCown | Byron Buxton | OF | MIN |
| 79 | Matthew Pouliot | Ketel Marte | 2B | ARI |
| 80 | Dave Shovein | Max Fried | SP | NYY |
| 81 | Frank Ammirante | Manny Machado | 3B | SD |
| 82 | James Schiano | Payton Tolle | SP | BOS |
| 83 | Justin Mason | Seiya Suzuki | OF | CHC |
| 84 | Jorge Montanez | Josh Hader | RP | HOU |
Round 7 gave us quite the run on outfielders. After Wyatt Langford ended last round, Henry Bolte, Riley Greene, Andy Pages, Ceddanne Rafaela, Byron Buxton, and Seiya Suzuki all came off the board in the seventh round. Bolte is the name that probably stands out. The Athletics’ rookie hit .277/.359/.405 in 119 big league games with 11 home runs and 21 steals. In 65 games in the second half, Bolte hit .289/.370/.448 with eight of his home runs and a 9.2% barrel rate. Bolte has always had loud raw tools, but he has struggled to lift the ball consistently, which has limited his power output. We started to see that a little more from him in the second half and, if it carries over, he has the makings of a 20/30 hitter in a great ballpark. Pat taking him at 73 means Bolte kind of HAS to get close to that in order to return value, which makes the pick a bit of a risk but not one without some logic to it.
The Buxton and Suzuki picks have their own risk too, along with clear upside. Buxton, who was coming off his best season in years, was limited to just 93 games because of a hip injury that ultimately required surgery. He’ll be 33 years old next season, with just one season over 105 games played since 2017 and coming off major hip surgery. A bit on him inside the top 80 is a huge risk, but we also know Buxton can produce fantasy value in 80-100 games. Suzuki is less of an injury risk but more of a team context risk since we have no idea where he’ll be playing next year. Perhaps it could provide a boost to his home run potential. Maybe the team context will limit his counting stats. We won’t know that for a while.
Two more starting pitchers also go here in Max Fried (SP21) and Payton Tolle (SP22), and, spoiler alert, one of them looks like a huge steal. When my starting pitching rankings come out later this week, I will have Tolle in my top 10 starting pitchers. He’ll be slotted right ahead of a tier of aces who have a history of injury (Crochet, Sale, deGrom, Wheeler), so maybe you want to call Tolle a top 15 starter if you’d take all of those injury risks over him. Still, getting a potential top 15 starting pitcher with pick 82 is tremendous. In case you think top-15 is rich for Tolle, he finished as the SP25 this season, and that was while recording just nine wins in 26 starts. He had a 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 28.4% strikeout rate and will be just 24 years old next season. As his breaking balls continue to develop, his performance should only improve.
| Round 8 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 85 | Jorge Montanez | Zack Gelof | 2B/OF | OAK |
| 86 | Justin Mason | Chase DeLauter | OF | CLE |
| 87 | James Schiano | Aroldis Chapman | RP | BOS |
| 88 | Frank Ammirante | Hunter Brown | SP | HOU |
| 89 | Dave Shovein | Freddie Freeman | 1B | LAD |
| 90 | Matthew Pouliot | Louis Varland | RP | TOR |
| 91 | Rivers McCown | Mason Montgomery | RP | PIT |
| 92 | Scott Pianowski | Mookie Betts | SS | LAD |
| 93 | D.J. Short | Tyler Soderstrom | 1B/OF | OAK |
| 94 | Frank Stampfl | Bryan Baker | RP | TB |
| 95 | George Bissell | Grant Taylor | RP | CHW |
| 96 | Roto Pat | JJ Wetherholt | SS | STL |
After Josh Hader went off the board in the last round as RP5, we got a run on closers here in the eighth round with Aroldis Chapman (RP6), Louis Varland (RP7), Mason Montgomery (RP8), Bryan Baker (RP9), and Grant Taylor (RP10). Hader and Chapman are the two established names among the group and make clear sense here, and Baker tied for the MLB lead in saves this season and will return for the potential World Series champion Rays. I’d say that makes him a solid top-ten closer. The other three are all bets on upside, and all bets that make sense. Varland was electric as a closer for the Blue Jays this season and finished as RP3 on the year. Taylor and Montgomery weren’t even full-time closers, and they finished as RP6 and RP7, respectively, due to their high innings totals and strikeout rates. The potential issue for both Taylor and Montgomery is that we have no idea if they will be used as traditional closers. Montgomery feels like the better bet since he had 18 saves this season, but it also took the Pirates a while to turn the role over to him, and they may prefer him in the “fireman” role in the same way the White Sox seem to prefer Taylor. That said, both of them are dominant relief arms.
Three young hitters also went in this round with Zack Gelof, Chase DeLauter, and JJ Wetherholt. Wetherholt as a top 100 pick after his rookie season makes sense, and DeLauter also clearly has the profile of a top 10 pick. His issue has been, and always will be, health risk. Yet, he did manage to play 133 games this season, hitting .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs and 11 steals. The hard-hit rates suggest that more power could be coming if he can lift the ball a bit more consistently.
Jorge’s pick of Gelof is also a bet that the 26-year-old really did reinvent himself this season, when he hit .256/.322/.475 with 22 home runs and 16 steals in 111 games. Gelof chased less outside of the zone, took a more patient approach overall, made more contact than he ever has, and was less pull-happy than he had been previously. All of that seems to suggest very real growth. Can the growth hold? That will be the big question you have to ask yourself if you draft him in the top 85 picks next season.
We also saw Hunter Brown go off the board here as SP23. If you had told people in March that you’d get Hunter Brown near the end of the eighth round, it would have seemed like a major coup. However, the Astros ace returned from a shoulder injury this season and never looked like himself. Is the injury still lingering, or was 2025 a bit of a fluke? Remember that he had a 3.49 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 25% strikeout rate in 2024. There was a major jump forward in 2025, but much of that was in the first half of the season. Even though his ratios remained strong after the All-Star break in 2025, his strikeout rate fell to 24%. So maybe Brown is more of a low 3.00-ERA pitcher who will post a 26% strikeout rate. That’s not a bad profile, but it’s not a top 15 arm. Then you have the health questions to factor in as well, so his slide here makes a bit of sense to me.
item.category: Yankees vs Red Sox Wild Card

item.title: [fansided.com] Ranking Tarik Skubal suitors from favorites to dark horses
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected. The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2
item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected.
The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2027. Really regardless of how MLB's labor dispute plays out, however, Los Angeles will hope to retain Skubal, who is still rightly regarded as the most bankable ace in baseball. The question is: Are the Dodgers the favorites for his services? Let's rank all realistic suitors, from least to most realistic.
8. Philadelphia Phillies
The Phillies are desperate and the Phillies typically spend money. Not necessarily as liberally as fans would like, but it's not impossible to imagine Dave Dombrowski — with the World Series window closing rapidly on this aging core — deciding that Skubal is worth an all-in push.
It would give Philadelphia the most talented rotation in MLB between Skubal, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Aaron Nola, four of whom could compete for NL Cy Young next season. There's also Andrew Painter, a former top prospect who came into his own down the stretch and delivered big outs in the postseason, to provide depth.
The Phillies probably have enough money wrapped up in that rotation (and in Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner) to be turned off of paying Skubal top dollar, but it's a fun thought for a team hoping to lean even more on run prevention moving forward.
7. Boston Red Sox
The Red Sox wielded one of the deepest and most reliable rotations in MLB last season; that was with top ace Garrett Crochet on the IL. Upon Crochet's return, Boston will have a compelling blend of experience (Crochet, Ranger Suárez) and emerging youth (Payton Tolle, Jake Bennett) to throw at their opponents.
Then again, they know the toll injuries can take, and Sonny Gray — probably their best regular season starter this past season — is now a free agent. The Red Sox could simply line up a new contract for Gray and be content, but why not aim higher? Skubal has proven remarkably durable over the years and he offers Boston a much longer window as Crochet's partner in crime. Suddenly, the Red Sox have the best one-two punch in baseball and it wouldn't be especially close.
After the Yankees lit them up in the Wild Card round (and after Boston's top arms couldn't pitch deep into either postseason game), there's pressure for a big swing.
6. Chicago Cubs
There's no doubting the Cubs' ability to generate offense, but the rotation has been a sore spot for years now. Jed Hoyer has shown a great appetite for spending in free agency of late; the Alex Bregman signing was a real flex. That said, Chicago needs to allocate more resources toward pitching. The Edward Cabrera trade went belly up. Shōta Imanaga is a free agent now, as are trade deadline pickups Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.
Chicago will get help internally with both Cade Horton and Justin Steele returning from season-long elbow injuries; Ben Brown, who finally broke out in 2026, should also be back in the mix. Beyond them, however, it's pretty grim. Matthew Boyd and Javier Assad can eat innings in the regular season, but neither has proven able to pitch deep in October — at least not consistently.
Skubal would deliver Chicago the frontline ace it has long lacked, with a solid scaffolding of talent behind him. The Cubs would be much better positioned to challenge Milwaukee in the division and potentially emerge from a crowded National League field.
5. Detroit Tigers
Skubal has made it clear he would've spent his entire career in Detroit if it was up to him. All the Tigers need to do is come through with a competitive offer. While last year's surprise Framber Valdez signing was a positive indication of the front office's competitive intent, there's a reason no Skubal extension ever came to fruition — or even remotely close.
A client of Scott Boras, Skubal was never inclined to sign an extension. But the Tigers' offers weren't even in the parking lot, much less the ballpark. Detroit will need to scale up its ambition significantly if it wants to lure Skubal back to the midwest.
All that said, Skubal has an affection for Detroit that's worth mentioning. The Tigers also desperately need a frontline ace in Skubal's mold. Young bucks like Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan are very talented, but the Tigers don't really have an established vet besides Valdez, who was a mess last season.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees tend to flex their muscles in free agency, although with diminishing returns in recent years. New York is no longer the most lucrative destination for a lot of A-tier stars. Juan Soto a couple years ago, Kyle Tucker last winter; the Yankees are getting outbid pretty consistently these days. That has not stopped New York from stockpiling stars, though, especially in the rotation.
It would require Hal Steinbrenner and the front office to basically sign off on a blank check, but the Yankees' ALDS loss to the Rays was a sobering defeat. There are cracks in the foundation. Many of those cracks are injury-related and concentrated in the lineup; Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón is as strong a four-man gauntlet as any rotation in MLB. The Yankees also have Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and top prospects like Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange for depth.
Still, the Yankees know the importance of depth, especially as their non-Schlittler core ages and becomes more injury-prone. Skubal provides stability and instantly lends credibility to any postseason aspirations. Schlittler-Skubal becomes the most fearsome pitching duo in baseball. Never say never.
3. Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays have steadily become the most aggressive front office in the American League. After finishing runner-up in the Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani sweepstakes, Toronto extended Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at a $500 million price point and signed Dylan Cease in the early days of free agency last winter. A disappointing season should not preclude Toronto from maintaining its all-in approach; if anything, it's more motivation for the Blue Jays to stack talent. This team was in the World Series a year ago.
Toronto is a great market, with a vibrant local culture and an entire country behind the Blue Jays. That ought to appeal to the vanity of a star like Skubal, who would team up with the projected AL Cy Young runner-up in Cease. The Jays also made a savvy trade for José Soriano at the deadline, adding another premium arm in his prime. Trey Yesavage, once healthy, could resume his ascent to stardom. The talent is there.
Skubal solidifies Toronto as a legitimate World Series contender coming into 2027. Moreover, the Jays have a lot of money coming off the books, which should free up the front office to spend recklessly where it counts. Toronto is always the "dark horse" in these top-dollar bidding wars, but ruling out the Blue Jays would be foolish.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
It's impossible to rule out the incumbents. Los Angeles made the Skubal trade in part because of their deep farm system — and in part because it set the stage for a potential long-term partnership. There's a reason small-market front offices were unwilling to match L.A.'s outgoing package (see: Brewers). The Dodgers could afford to trade two of the 50ish best prospects in baseball because the team can feel reasonably good about both competing for a World Series this season (oh well) and re-signing Skubal when he hits the open market.
An NLCS loss does complicate the situation somewhat, not to mention the unknowability of upcoming labor disputes. The Dodgers' loss was a direct result of investing hundreds of millions of dollars in stars who are beginning to decline. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell are all on the wrong side of 30; Tucker will join that list next season. Los Angeles will endure more and more diminishing returns.
That said, nothing (besides a strict salary cap) can really stop the Dodgers from compensating for declining stars by signing more expensive stars, even if it leaves the cap sheet in utter chaos five years from now. That has been L.A.'s strategy to date; it was part of the logic behind the Skubal trade. The Dodgers still arguably represent Skubal's best chance to win a World Series, which will no doubt be part of the calculus if another team can't dramatically outspend them.
1. New York Mets
If any team can blow L.A.'s offer out of the water, it's the Mets. Steve Cohen is baseball's richest owner and New York has consistently tossed its hat in the ring for MLB's premium free agents. Juan Soto's $765 million contract set a new record; Skubal very well could set a record for pitchers.
The Mets are coming off of a last-place season, too, which only fuels anxiety in the fan base. It should also fuel aggression in the front office. David Stearns is under pressure to prove that he has what it takes to win in New York. Skubal would join an emerging ace in Nolan McLean, plus other whippersnappers like Zac Thornton and Jonah Tong. The Mets need depth besides, as Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea look more like bullpen arms these days. New York, however, is the one non-Dodgers team with enough money to sign Skubal and pursue other targets.
If the Dodgers get spooked by the shadow of their own payroll, which is more likely than ever, the Mets are the logical team we can expect to swoop in and win the Skubal bidding war outright.
