item.title: [Yahoo Sports] The Philadelphia Phillies Don't Actually Need Tarik Skubal
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies absolutely need to bolster their roster this offseason after yet another early playoff exit, but they actually shouldn't be pursuing the biggest fish on the free-agent market. Tarik Skubal is going to be the top player available this winter, and he will surely have a wide range of suitors. But the Phillies should not be one of them. Why? Because Philadelphia already boasts one of the best starting rotations in baseball. The trio of Cristopher Sanchez, Jesus Luzardo and
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies absolutely need to bolster their roster this offseason after yet another early playoff exit, but they actually shouldn't be pursuing the biggest fish on the free-agent market.
Tarik Skubal is going to be the top player available this winter, and he will surely have a wide range of suitors. But the Phillies should not be one of them.
Why? Because Philadelphia already boasts one of the best starting rotations in baseball.
The trio of Cristopher Sanchez, Jesus Luzardo and Zack Wheeler is fantastic, and Andrew Painter showed tremendous signs during the second half of the season.
Yes, Aaron Nola is infinitely replaceable, but he did have a strong second half overall, even if his last couple of starts were less than desirable.
Skubal is likely to command $400 million. He's one of the best pitchers in baseball, he's a left-hander and his agent is Scott Boras.
The Phillies have already been monitoring their payroll closely as it is. Their roster is littered with lucrative long-term deals, some of which are not exactly good ones. Do they really want to spend nearly half a billion dollars in an area that doesn't have a need?
Philadelphia needs bats and it needs relievers; period. The Phillies had one of the worst offenses in the league this year, and their bullpen was a disaster down the stretch — and really, for most of the campaign.
That is where Philadelphia should be spending its money.
Sure, the idea of Skubal is tempting. He is a dominant force who won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and just posted a 2.72 ERA and 0.964 WHIP in 2026.
But he's also turning 30 years old next month and has had multiple elbow surgeries. Handing him big-time money over an extended period of time is going to be a significant risk, and it's one that the Phillies really can't take.
Philadelphia's holes are obvious. It must address its outfield, which didn't field a single reliable hitter this season. It needs to find another bat either at second base or third base, depending on where the Phillies want to put Bryson Stott. And they also need to bring in a serviceable catcher alongside J.T. Realmuto.
And of course, it must build a better bridge to Jhoan Duran in the ninth inning.
Skubal does not fill any of those needs. At that cost, it's simply not worth it.

item.content:encoded:
Skip to content
Sorry, Phillies fans, Dave Dombrowski is not going anywhere for a long, long time. Is that a bad thing?
Dealin' Dave, President for Life, denied offering a job to Alex Cora, said Trea Turner must audition at shortstop, and said the farm system is A-OK. Seriously: I hope John Middleton never fires him.
If you’re a Dave Dombrowski hater, no matter where you were or what you were doing, your blood ran cold Thursday morning. That was when the Phillies president of baseball operations, in his post-season news conference, blithely remarked:
“I plan on being here for a while. I enjoy it. I’m healthy. I have quality people around me.”
In a town whose football team has lost three straight and whose coach blew the last game in the last 8 seconds; whose basketball team hasn’t gotten past the second round of the playoffs in 25 years; and whose hockey team is winless in its first nine games, Dombrowski is, by far, the most despised sports figure.
And he’s here for the long haul.
Marcus Hayes alerts
During his 61-minute, end-of-season news conference, Dombrowski addressed important issues: Trea Turner’s pending and overdue removal from the shortstop position; his unwillingness to trade from among the starting pitching but his willingness to trade star hitters if those hitters were willing; announcements that Don Mattingly will return as manager and turnover on the coaching staff; and his faith in a minor-league system that he believes is incorrectly rated among the worst in baseball.
But his own future, both long- and short-term, was the most significant issue of the day.
Is that a bad thing? Most Phillies fans, in this moment, would answer, resoundingly, “Yes.”
The backstory
Dombrowski took the Phillies to the World Series in 2022, his second season, but playoff collapses in the following four seasons authored mainly by Dombrowski’s porous bullpens and choking hitters put a target on his back that even José Alvarado could hit. This year, as the Phillies faded from the top wild-card slot to the final wild-card slot to a three-game wild-card exit in Atlanta, Dombrowski’s star sank lower than ever in every corner of Philadelphia ... except one. It’s the only corner that matters.
It’s the office of John Middleton, the Phillies’ managing partner.
Middleton adores Dombrowski. Last month, following up a report by The Athletic that Dombrowski will soon receive an extension beyond his current deal’s expiration in 2027, I was told by a Phillies source, “Middleton will never fire Dombrowski.”
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly ‘carried the stick.’ That helped make him the best choice as Phillies manager.
A few days later, USA Today reported that the Phillies will offer Dombrowski a lifetime contract, presumably to fill whatever role he desires. Right now, at the age of 70, he still desires to decide who’s on the roster and who’s managing them.
Has he earned it? Not in Philadelphia, no. But elsewhere, Dombrowski won two World Series and went to two more. Middleton adores him; essentially, in Middleton’s eyes, Dombrowski can do no wrong.
In my eyes, Dombrowski’s been about average. He inherited an organization that included Bryce Harper, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Aaron Nola, J.T. Realmuto, Alec Bohm, and Bryson Stott.
He’s extended some of those deals, signed Kyle Schwarber (twice), enhanced the roster with trades for Jesús Luzardo and Jhoan Duran, and hit on deadline deals for Harrison Bader in 2025 and Luis Arraez in 2026 (both were hurt in the playoffs, though).
He also has consistently failed to replace the right-handed power of Rhys Hoskins, has shown abominable judgment in bullpen construction, and, in seeking optimal offensive output, has inexcusably and illogically devalued defense, especially for a team so heavily invested in big-money starting pitching: He has four $100 million starters.
Further, the contracts of outfielder Nick Castellanos, a defensive liability, Turner, a defensive liability, and starter Taijuan Walker, the ultimate defensive liability, proved utterly indefensible.
Still, as Middleton loves to point out, any president who takes a team to the playoffs five years in a row must be doing something right.
» READ MORE: To Dave Dombrowski, the Phillies’ problems begin an arm’s length away
Counterpoint: In Dombrowski’s case, so far, most of what he’s done right is that he hasn’t messed with what former GM Matt Klentak left him.
Also: If the Phillies are such a quality team with such a bright future, why did Alex Cora, the manager who won Dombrowski the 2018 World Series in Boston, turn down the manager’s job twice in six months? Does he want to win Puerto Rico the Father of the Year this badly?
Furthermore, if Dombrowski was such a hotshot executive, why did the Sox fire him less than 11 months after winning it all?
None of those questions matter. What matters is, John hearts Dave.
Madness ensues
I, for one, am happy that Dombrowski is sticking around. That’s mainly because I, for one, don’t care if the Phillies win every game, lose every game, or have every game rained out, as long as they’re interesting while doing it.
Also, I enjoy talking to Dombrowski. He’s smart, intriguing, and his hair has its own aura, as the kids say.
Besides, how can I endorse firing a guy who I’m giving a grade like “C?” You know, average. You fire guys who get D’s and F’s.
That “C” grade means Dombrowski probably does a better job at roster building than, say, I, who am a connoisseur of shortstops (and point guards); a far better job than, say Mike Sielski, whose expertise is limited to hockey centermen; but probably not as good a job as David Murphy, who obsesses on wRC+ and FIP (and who, incongruently, is a quarterback aficionado, too).
» READ MORE: Phillies will keep Trea Turner at shortstop for now: ‘He knows he has to be better’
Also, Dombrowski says crazy stuff.
He fired Rob Thomson and, after being turned down by Cora, the fired former Red Sox manager, he replaced Thomson with Mattingly, the bench coach, as interim manager.
Dombrowski said Thursday that, while he’d followed a baseball mandate and interviewed other candidates, he had never offered the job to anyone but Mattingly. He said this with a straight face ... after both USA Today and the Phillies’ own website reported that, early last week, Cora had turned him down again.
Dombrowski on Thursday also said he actually signed Mattingly to a deal last Saturday, but, with the Eagles playing Sunday (24 hours later) and with Mattingly lacking solid internet service at his vacation lodgings, they delayed leaking the news until Wednesday ... so as to have better Wi-Fi on Thursday for Mattingly’s Zoom news conference.
I am not making any of that up.
Old MacDonald’s farm
Dombrowski also tried to convince listeners that their farm system is better than the experts rank it, which is generally between fifth-to-last and second-to-last. He asserted that major league rookies Andrew Painter, Justin Crawford, and Alex McFarlane should count toward their farm depth, and that they should be credited for using prospects to acquire Luzardo and Duran.
Dombrowski ignored the fact that Painter and Crawford did not factor into the current rankings at all, and he ignored the fact that teams ranked higher than his also traded prospects to improve. For instance, the Dodgers traded three prospects at the deadline to acquire Tarik Skubal from the Tigers, two of them ranked in the top 100 by MLB.com, and still had an elite system at the season’s end. The Brewers also traded prospects for bullpen help at the deadline, and their farm system remains as good or better than the Dodgers’ — whom they just swept out of the NLCS.
Coup de grace
The nuttiest thing Dombrowski said in his hourlong State of the Union regarded Turner. By most metrics, Turner was, by far, the worst defensive shortstop in all of baseball. Dombrowski’s solution:
He forced Turner to leave his home in Florida and travel to Philadelphia for a two-hour meeting with Dombrowski, which is like a kid on summer break getting called back to school to go to the principal’s office. What did they talk about for two hours? Some of it concerned Turner’s career-worst offensive performance, which is weird, since that’s kind of the job of the manager and the hitting coach. Some of it concerned Turner’s defense.
Dombrowski warned Turner that Turner would have to audition in spring training if he hopes to retain the shortstop job. Otherwise, he will be moved, most likely to left field, though Turner would prefer staying on the infield, most likely at second base.
» READ MORE: The most imaginative changes the Phillies can make begin with moving Trea Turner off shortstop
What?
WHAT?
So, the plan to return the 33-year-old’s defensive skills from putridity back to their heights, which were mediocrity, is to have him walk on eggshells for 20 spring training games? In which he will play, what, a total of 90 innings — 90 innings that Turner could spend acclimating himself to second base, where he’s started just 79 games, or left field where he’s played zero games?
Assume Turner exits spring training as the shortstop, then he commits four errors in April — again. Do you banish him to the grass or push him to the right side of the infield in the middle of the season? What chance does he have to succeed in that sort of atmosphere?
Of all the harebrained schemes the Phillies have hatched in the past 15 years or so, the plan for Turner is the wildest. Really, this stuff just writes itself. Thanks, Dave.
And, Mr. Middleton: To hell with your fans. For my sake, and for the sake of columnists everywhere, please never fire Dave Dombrowski.

item.title: [MLB.com] Bravos respaldan a Acuña en medio de su mala racha: “No tiene que ser Superman”
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Hubo una época en la que habría sido impensable que un manager rival le lanzara con cuidado a cualquier bateador para enfrentar al venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr. Pero también hubo un momento en el que habría parecido poco realista pensar que Acuña tendría las dificultades que ha experimentado en sus últimas dos postemporadas.
“Sólo necesitamos que Ronald sea Ronald”, dijo Chris Sale, as de los Bravos. “Seré sincero, el 50 por ciento de él es mejor que la mayoría. Creo que volver a casa podría aliviar un poco esa presión, estar frente a nuestros aficionados y simplemente mantenerse relajado. Creo que cuando llegas a estas situaciones, a veces intentas hacer de más”.
Acuña sentirá el cariño de la afición local en Truist Park el martes. Intentará ayudar a Atlanta a tomar ventaja de 2-1 en esta Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional, pactada al mejor de cinco juegos.
“No me preocupa, simplemente porque su talento es tan grande que en algún momento va a aparecer”, dijo Walt Weiss, manager de los Bravos.
No es que Acuña esté atravesando una mala racha prolongada. Simplemente está en una que se magnifica bajo las brillantes luces de la postemporada. Es el mismo jugador que registró un OPS de .997 en sus últimos 26 juegos de la temporada regular.
Pero en los primeros cinco juegos de esta postemporada, Acuña batea de 18-3, con tres boletos, tres ponches y ningún extrabase. También ha aportado valor con tres bases robadas.
Cabe señalar que durante ese gran cierre de temporada no estuvo enfrentándose a diario a lanzadores de la talla de Jesús Luzardo, Cristopher Sánchez, Tarik Skubal y Blake Snell. Pero la alta calidad del pitcheo no disminuye la frustración, especialmente cuando las dificultades en postemporada se remontan más allá de la campaña actual.
“Me encanta enfrentar a lanzadores que son superestrellas”, dijo Acuña. “Cada vez que voy al plato, voy a competir. Estamos tratando de ganar. Así que estoy haciendo lo mejor que puedo. Como saben, esos pitcheos son tremendos”.
Cuando Acuña bateó .337, registró un OPS de 1.017 y se convirtió en el primer jugador de la historia en sumar al menos 70 bases robadas en una temporada de 40 jonrones en el 2023, habría sido impensable que el manager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, hiciera lo que hizo en la victoria de Atlanta en el Juego 2.
Con corredores en segunda y tercera y un out en el octavo inning, Roberts ordenó a Roki Sasaki darle un boleto intencional a Drake Baldwin para preparar un enfrentamiento entre derechos contra Acuña. Tampoco es que Baldwin haya estado encendido. Su OPS de .484 en esta postemporada es, de hecho, inferior al de Acuña (.485). Pero la decisión de Roberts de lanzarle al bateador derecho dio resultado cuando Acuña bateó un rodado para una doble matanza que puso fin a la entrada.
“Creo que cada vez que ves a alguien pasar por algo así, te solidarizas con él porque casi sientes que está tratando de hacer demasiado o poniéndose demasiada presión”, dijo Sale.
Acuña tiene un OPS de .495 en las 39 apariciones al plato que ha registrado en postemporada desde el 2023. Esa cifra lo ubica en el puesto 108 entre 121 jugadores de MLB que han acumulado al menos 35 apariciones al plato en playoffs desde entonces.
Pero ciertamente no es la única superestrella que ha atravesado malas rachas prolongadas en la postemporada.
Pete Crow-Armstrong probablemente ganará el JMV de la Liga Nacional este año. Ocupa el puesto 120 en esa misma lista, con un OPS de .342 en 37 apariciones al plato. El primera base de los Bravos, Matt Olson, ha registrado un par de temporadas de 40 jonrones o más, pero aparece justo detrás de Acuña con un OPS de .490.
“Ronald es el mejor jugador del equipo y el más talentoso”, dijo Olson. “No tiene que ser Superman. Puede impactar el juego de muchísimas maneras. Todos confiamos plenamente en el jugador que es y en su talento”.

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
item.dc:creator: Joel Reuter
item.description: Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation Pitching wins championships. item.content:encoded:
Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros
1 of 12
RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP)
RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP)
RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP)
RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)
The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.
Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.
With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.
11. Chicago White Sox
2 of 12
RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP)
RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP)
RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP)
LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin
The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.
Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.
Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.
10. Chicago Cubs
3 of 12
LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP)
RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP)
LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP)
LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad
The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.
Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.
Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.
9. San Diego Padres
4 of 12
RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP)
RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP)
RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP)
LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez
The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.
Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.
Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.
8. Cleveland Guardians
5 of 12
RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP)
LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP)
RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP)
LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Foster Griffin
Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.
Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.
The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.
7. Atlanta Braves
6 of 12
LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP)
RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP)
RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)
Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.
Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.
Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.
6. Milwaukee Brewers
7 of 12
RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP)
RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP)
LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP)
RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan
Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.
Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.
Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.
5. Boston Red Sox
8 of 12
RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP)
LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP)
LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP)
RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval
Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.
Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.
The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.
4. Tampa Bay Rays
9 of 12
RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP)
RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP)
RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP)
RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)
Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.
That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.
They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.
3. Philadelphia Phillies
10 of 12
LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP)
RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP)
RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP)
LHP Jesús Luzardo (14-5, 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 221 K, 178.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Andrew Painter
Jesús Luzardo played catch earlier this week as he works his way back from shoulder inflammation, though his postseason status remains up in the air. There's a chance he will be limited to bullpen work early in the playoffs.
Veteran Aaron Nola has hit his stride of late, posting a 2.45 ERA in 66 innings over his last 11 starts, so he can fill the void behind the dynamic one-two punch of Cristopher Sánchez (7.7 WAR, 1st among all SP) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR, 8th among all SP).
The Phillies rank second in the majors with 73 quality starts and 869.1 innings from their starting staff, so they are poised to lean on their starters as hard as anyone in October.
2. New York Yankees
11 of 12
RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP)
LHP Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP, 104 K, 112.2 IP)
RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 131 K, 127.0 IP)
LHP Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 91 K, 84.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Will Warren
With AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and three established veteran starters capable of frontline production in Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, the Yankees rotation is capable of making a major impact in October.
Schlittler logged a 1.26 ERA over 14.1 innings last October, including eight scoreless frames against the rival Red Sox in the Wild Card Round. He will now be asked to shoulder a heavier load.
It remains to be seen who the odd-man out would be in a series that calls for a three-man staff, though Rodón has made his case with a 1.42 ERA, 0.75 WHIP and 28 strikeouts in 25.1 innings in September.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
12 of 12
RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9, 2.53 ERA, 0.87 WHIP, 182 K, 185.0 IP)
LHP Tarik Skubal (4-2, 2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP, 60 K, 55.0 IP)
LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.86 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 52 K, 38.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Glasnow (5-2, 3.53 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 98 K, 74.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Emmet Sheehan, LHP Justin Wrobleski
The Dodgers have once again navigated much of the regular season without Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, but they are healthy rolling into October and poised to round out the playoff rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto and deadline pickup Tarik Skubal.
The starting rotation logged a 2.68 ERA over 104 innings last postseason, with Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow starting 13 of 17 games and the rest going to Shohei Ohtani, who will be limited to DH duties but has been sufficiently replaced by a two-time Cy Young winner in Skubal.
Right-hander Emmet Sheehan has a 0.53 ERA and 24 strikeouts over 17 innings in three September starts. He will serve as a multi-inning weapon out of the bullpen.

item.title: [MLB.com] Braves-Dodgers NLDS Game 1 FAQ (4 p.m. ET, FOX/FOX One)
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen; Mark Bowman
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- The last time the Braves and Dodgers met in the postseason, a trip to the World Series was on the line. The Braves ousted the Dodgers in the 2021 NL Championship Series, going on to win the fourth championship in franchise history. But since then, Atlanta has not made it past the Division Series round, while L.A. is the defending back-to-back champion. The Dodgers' three-peat bid will begin in earnest when they take on the Braves in the 2026 NL Division Series starting this Saturd
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The last time the Braves and Dodgers met in the postseason, a trip to the World Series was on the line.
The Braves ousted the Dodgers in the 2021 NL Championship Series, going on to win the fourth championship in franchise history. But since then, Atlanta has not made it past the Division Series round, while L.A. is the defending back-to-back champion.
The Dodgers' three-peat bid will begin in earnest when they take on the Braves in the 2026 NL Division Series starting this Saturday afternoon at Dodger Stadium, with triple-digit heat in the forecast.
During the regular season, the Braves outplayed the Dodgers, winning five of their six meetings and outscoring them 26-15. But the postseason is a different beast, and a rested L.A. club will meet an Atlanta team that had to play hard to eliminate Philadelphia from the best-of-three Wild Card Series.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 1 is set for 4 p.m. ET/1 p.m. PT on Saturday at Dodger Stadium. It will be broadcast on FOX, FOX Deportes and FOX ONE.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Braves: TBD
Injuries have depleted Atlanta's rotation. Chris Sale won’t be available before Game 2 on Sunday, and Tyler Mahle won’t be available before Game 3 on Tuesday. As for Martín Pérez, who was placed on the injured list with low back inflammation on Sept. 1, he couldn’t be activated before Game 3. Grant Holmes threw just two innings in Thursday’s win over the Phillies, so he may be asked to pitch the first few innings. Or, the Braves could go with Brent Suter as an opener and have Holmes follow.
Yamamoto had already established himself as a big-game pitcher long before arriving in the Majors, but he took it to another level last postseason when he tossed consecutive complete games in the NLCS and the World Series before closing out the winner-take-all Game 7 on zero days' rest. Yamamoto taking the ball in Game 1 would be the only way to have him available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: Michael Harris II, Matt Olson and Drake Baldwin will have to contend with a lefty in Skubal again after facing two left-handed starters in Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez during the Wild Card Series.
Dodgers: After Shohei Ohtani recovered from right biceps and left knee injuries and returned from the 15-day IL, manager Dave Roberts began using a platoon in the leadoff spot, slotting in Ohtani against right-handers and Mookie Betts against left-handers. The leadoff platoon, as well as other tweaks corresponding to the handedness of the opposing starter, is expected to continue in the postseason.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Braves: Didier Fuentes might be the only reliever who isn’t available. He pitched three consecutive days during the Wild Card Series. Robert Suarez has surrendered an extra-base hit in each of the three appearances he’s had since his right elbow inflammation forced him to the injured list in June. But his velocity was up and he looked more like himself while throwing two-thirds of an inning Thursday. He’ll likely get some high-leverage spots, especially with Dylan Lee struggling most of the second half and into the postseason.
Dodgers: L.A. may not have a set closer this postseason, but Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz all seem to be viable ninth-inning options. Righty reliever Edgardo Henriquez, whose regular season ended early due to a lower back strain, is expected to be activated for the NLDS as long as he comes out of bye week workouts feeling good, bolstering the Dodgers' already solid mix of leverage arms.
Any injuries of note?
Dodgers: Of the players who ended the season on the IL, the Dodgers are most confident about Henriquez returning. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option.
Who is hot and who is not?
Braves: Olson, Albies and Harris all homered in Thursday’s win over the Phillies. Harris went 5-for-11 in the Wild Card Series. Baldwin went 2-for-13 and Acuña was 1-for-9.
Dodgers: In September, Betts (1.112 OPS) and Teoscar Hernández (.965 OPS) were two of the Dodgers' hottest hitters. Tucker (.890 OPS) had his best month by far in his disappointing first season in L.A., perhaps getting hot at the right time.
Freeman dealt with right patellar tendinitis early last month, and he has slugged just .355 since the beginning of July. Ohtani recorded a .666 OPS in his past 29 games, when his biceps and knee injuries flared up and impacted his performance.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Dodgers are bidding for the fifth three-peat in World Series history, and the first since the 1998-2000 Yankees. They would be the first National League team to pull off the feat.
• The Braves and Dodgers will be meeting in the postseason for the sixth time. Atlanta was victorious in the 1996 NLDS and the 2021 NLCS. Los Angeles won the 2013 NLDS, 2018 NLDS and 2020 NLCS.

item.content:encoded:
Will we be able to see Kim Ha-seong (Atlanta Braves) and Kim Hye-seong (LA Dodgers) face off on the big league postseason stage? Kim Hye-seong looks likely to join the postseason roster for a second consecutive year.
North American sports outlet 'The Athletic' included Kim Hye-seong's name when projecting the Dodgers' division series roster on the 3rd (Korea time).
Defensive utility ability and his quick feet are the reasons Kim Hye-seong is expected to be included on the postseason roster. The outlet predicted a 26-man roster composed of 15 position players and 11 pitchers. The position player entries would be two catchers (Will Smith, Hunter Pﬂueger), four infielders (Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Max Muncy), three outfielders (Teoscar Hernández, Kyle Tucker, Andy Pages), two utilities (Tommy Edman, Kiké Hernández), and one designated hitter (Shohei Ohtani). It also projected that rookie Hosuey de Paula would take on the pinch-hitting role and Kim Hye-seong would serve as a pinch runner.
Reporter Fabian Ardaya explained, "Kim Hye-seong being on this list is not because of his hitting. He can run faster than anyone in the infield group, the oldest position group in Major League Baseball. Also, if late in the game the team inserts Hosuey de Paula and must remove one player to make two substitutions, Kim Hye-seong can cover infield defense."
Reporter KT Woo said, "Do you want an example that shows how important one stolen base can be in the postseason? Then ask manager Dave Roberts." Roberts recorded a steal that will be remembered in postseason history. The comment projected that Kim Hye-seong could be used as a late-game joker.
Kim Hye-seong finished the season in Triple-A after failing to return to the major leagues since May. His Triple-A performance was not very good either. But with everyone aware of Kim Hye-seong's speed, there is a mood that does not ignore his utility as a short-series specialist.
Manager Roberts is deliberating. At a press conference with local reporters on the 3rd he explained, "The point to consider is bench resources. We have to decide which additional players to take, whether to include a pinch runner. We're trying to coordinate that. The final bullpen pitcher spot is also under consideration."
If Kim Hye-seong is included in the division series roster, we could see a Korean derby in the postseason alongside Atlanta's Kim Ha-seong. Kim Ha-seong was already included on the Philadelphia Phillies' wild-card series roster and started in games 1 and 2.
Philadelphia started left-handed starters Jesus Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez, giving the right-handed Kim Ha-seong opportunities in a platoon role. For now, the Dodgers' Game 1 starter is also left-hander Tarik Skubal. Blake Snell is also expected to start Game 2. In that case, Kim Ha-seong could appear in both starting lineups.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Should the Phillies trade Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Why blockbuster deal doesn't make sense
item.dc:creator: Matt Snyder
item.description: The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday. It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so
item.content:encoded:
The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday.
It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so I get it. It happens. We're often prisoners of the moment and emotion is a real thing.
I do want to push back on a specific idea, though, as floated by Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic:
Trading Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Don't love the idea, but everything needs to be under consideration. Everything.
Now, be sure that this isn't to attack the writer there, as I have the utmost respect for him and he even said he doesn't love the idea. I can see a lot of people running with this, though, and I'll offer up my opinion that this just isn't a feasible idea for the Phillies.
First off, Harper has a no-trade clause and it's been pretty clear over the last several years that he's now Philly through-and-through and doesn't want to go anywhere. Schwarber also has a no-trade clause with his 10-and-5 rights and now has a family with two young children.
Let's say either or both would accept a trade. Would it help the Phillies other than salary relief?
Schwarber is a 34-year-old designated hitter heading into 2027 with four years and $132 million left on his deal. How many teams would give the Phillies anything of value while also taking on a large portion of the salary? The answer is not that many and it might be zero.
Harper needs to permanently go back to first base and he'll also be 34 years old next season. He has five years and roughly $125 million left on his deal. Again, how many teams would give good value back to the Phillies and salary relief? The number is higher than with Schwarber, but not by much.
This isn't to say neither player is good. Both are very productive offensively. In fact, they were the Phillies' only two good hitters this season. Harper had a 131 OPS+ and Schwarber was at 128 with 100 being the average player at getting on base and hitting for power. No other qualified players on the Phillies were in the vicinity of Harper or Schwarber. Only Bryson Stott at 98 even approached league average. Brandon Marsh finished at 90, Alec Bohm 87 and Trea Turner 81. Yuck.
Schwarber and Harper are much more valuable to the Phillies than they would be to any other team, given the circumstances. And, unless the Phillies are going full-on rebuild, they might as well play out the contracts and try to win with them.
If you look at how things are set up for next season with the pitching staff, a rebuild doesn't make sense.
- Jesús Luzardo made a turn toward ace this season. He's under team control through at least 2031.
- Cristopher Sánchez will likely finish in the top three of Cy Young voting. He's under team control through at least 2032.
- Zack Wheeler showed flashes of being really good while returning from an incredibly tough surgical procedure. He's signed for one more season. He could well return to ace form.
- Aaron Nola doesn't have a tradeable deal, but hey, he had a 10-start stretch with a 2.10 ERA late in the season.
- There were still inconsistencies, but Andrew Painter, at age 23, made big strides during the season and perhaps turned a corner with in Game 2 vs. the Braves. Next year could well be a breakout.
That's a five-man rotation and maybe one of the very best in the majors.
Jhoan Duran is a top-three closer, too.
The starting point here is a great rotation and closer combination, along with Harper and Schwarber being excellent hitters. That's a better nucleus than most teams have. Ownership is committed to doing what it takes to land a winner for the city of Philadelphia and Dave Dombrowski is a front office executive who has proven he's good at making good teams into champions.
Keep taking as many shots at the postseason as possible in hopes that one of these years, the hot streak lines up properly for a championship. We've seen a well-timed hot streak pay off in recent years for teams like the Nationals, Braves and Rangers -- and maybe it'll be the Padres this year? -- so we know it can happen. Hell, the 2022 Phillies were right there.
The team defense needs to improve and there should be some tinkering with the position players, but the foundation here is far too strong to bail on Schwarber and/or Harper, especially when it wouldn't improve the big-league roster in the near-term.

item.title: [nbcphiladelphia.com] Phillies' season ends with the pain of another early postseason knockout
item.dc:creator: Jim Salisbury
item.description: ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport. A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers. A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter. It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport.
A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers.
A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter.
It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was tagged for three runs in the first inning. The Phillies never recovered. Their season came to an end in a 6-2 loss to the Braves in Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series.
For just the second time in franchise history, the Phillies qualified for the postseason for a fifth straight year, matching a team-high streak first reached from 2007 to 2011. The Phils won the World Series in 2008, but have not since. They made a surprising run to the World Series in 2022 but were beaten by the Houston Astros in six games. They were a win away from returning to the World Series in 2023 only to collapse and lose Games 6 and 7 of the NL Championship Series at home to Arizona. Since then, they have gone the wrong way, losing in the Division Series (their first round of play) in 2024 and 2025 and now in the Wild Card Series.
“It’s always frustrating,” Kyle Schwarber said in the quiet of the losing clubhouse. “From every postseason I’ve been in, it always hurts when you’re not the last team standing.
“It’s just as frustrating this year as it was last year and the year before that.”
Philadelphia Phillies
Complete coverage of the Fightin' Phils and their MLB rivals from NBC Sports Philadelphia.
As the October defeats have mounted, the team’s core group of high-priced veteran players has gotten older.
Schwarber, always the optimist, insisted that the team’s championship window is still wide open. So did J.T. Realmuto, saying, “There’s definitely the talent in this room to win. If you watched us play all year, no matter who we played, we weren’t outmatched. It’s about execution. It’s not about the age and the years. We know we still have the talent to win.”
Over on the other side of the clubhouse, Bryce Harper didn’t sound so sure.
He was asked what gives him faith that the team can still get to where it wants to go.
“Yeah, I don’t know,” he said. “It’s going to be a long offseason, obviously. I have trust in the organization and the people that are in charge. We’ll see where we go.”
Heading into the offseason, the Phils have many questions, first and foremost: Will Don Mattingly return as manager in 2027? He took over, with an interim tag, for Rob Thomson after the team got off to a 9-19 start in April.
The Phillies played .590 ball (79-55) under Mattingly, but president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski tried to hire Alex Cora when he let Thomson go, and he seems likely to try again in the coming weeks. Stay tuned.
Mattingly would not touch the topic after the game. Schwarber, Realmuto, Nola and Trea Turner all said they’d like to see Mattingly return. Harper declined to talk about the topic.
If Cora comes on board, he will be taking over a team of highs and lows, one with an inconsistent offense that is seemingly up one month (see August) and down the next (see September). He will be taking over a team that lacks pitching depth, both in the starting rotation and the bullpen. Both weaknesses reared their head in recent weeks as the Phils had to scramble to make the playoffs, using ace Zack Wheeler on the final day of the regular season, a circumstance that prevented him from starting Game 1 of the postseason.
Wheeler mentioned the team’s overall inconsistency when asked if he believed the Phils still had the talent to make a deeper postseason run next year.
“Consistency in every group, I think that’s what will get us there,” he said. “We were kind of inconsistent throughout the year. Maybe we were hitting, but we weren’t pitching well. Maybe we were pitching well and we weren’t hitting well. We just have to put it all together throughout the majority of the season.
“We’re hungry, that’s for sure. We just didn’t get the job done.”
The Phils had chances to win the series.
Jesus Luzardo pitched well in Game 1 and they held a 3-2 lead in the seventh. With few trusted arms in his leaky bullpen, Mattingly went to his All-Star closer, Jhoan Duran, in the bottom of the seventh. Duran got through that inning but gave up the lead on a three-run homer in the eighth and the Phillies lost, 5-3.
They bounced back to win a wild Game 2 Wednesday in 10 innings on the strength of three late home runs and the clutch pitching of Cristopher Sanchez, Alex McFarlane and Andrew Painter. They seemed to have momentum heading into Game 3.
But the momentum disappeared quickly as Nola had big trouble throwing strikes.
Just three of the right-hander's first 13 pitches to open the game were strikes. He fell behind Ronald Acuna Jr., and Matt Olson, the Braves’ Nos. 2 and 3 hitters, with 3-0 counts and eventually walked both. He then fell behind Michael Harris II, 2-0. Harris hit the next pitch, a sinker down and out of the zone, over the right-field wall for a three-run homer.
“I think he was just a little too careful,” Realmuto said of Nola. “I don’t think he was way off because he was just missing. They just did a good job of not chasing and making him come in the zone. When a lineup is good like that and they get on a roll, it’s tough to get them out when they’re not chasing.”
Nola did not make it through the second inning. Tim Mayza got the final out of the frame before handing off to Wheeler in the top of the third. The Phillies’ brain trust opted not to start Wheeler on three days’ rest. He'd never done that before. Also, Wheeler admitted that at this point of the season, he wasn’t feeling 100 percent. It was decided that Nola’s best chance of succeeding would be to stay in a starter’s role.
“We’re going to need Nola in this game,” Mattingly said before the game. “Starting him gives us the best version of him.”
The Phillies weren’t sure Wheeler would even be able to pitch until he tested himself by playing catch before the game. He ended up pitching four innings but was not particularly sharp. He gave up three hits and walked three. One of those walks turned into a run when Ozzie Albies stroked a two-run homer in the fourth to give the Braves a 5-0 lead.
“We felt Nola was on solid rest,” Mattingly said after the game. “If he could get us into the game at all, we’d have Zack after that. Obviously, it didn’t go well.”
Atlanta used lefty Ray Kerr as an opener. He pitched 3 1/3 innings and did not allow a run. The only hit Kerr gave up was a single to Schwarber in the first inning. Kerr then struck out Harper.
Grant Holmes, Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes, Dylan Dodd and Chris Sale finished off the Phillies. Sale, the Braves’ ace lefty who started Game 1, entered with two outs in the eighth and struck out Harper.
Before the 2019 season, Harper signed a 13-year, $330-million contract with the Phillies. He came looking for a parade down Broad Street. Eight years later, he boarded a flight back to Philadelphia, still looking.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] MLB Playoff Roundup: Alec Bohm’s 10th-inning homer forces Game 3 against Braves

item.description: What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa. The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the post
item.content:encoded:
What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

item.content:encoded:
Phillies' Aaron Nola Reportedly Starting vs. Braves over Zack Wheeler For MLB Playoffs Series Finale
The Philadelphia Phillies will go into Thursday's winner-take-all Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card series with Aaron Nola starting on the mound.
Per The Athletic's Matt Gelb, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly is going with Nola rather than using Zack Wheeler on short rest with a spot in the NLDS at stake.
As a result of their four-game losing streak last week that prevented them from clinching a playoff spot early, the Phillies had to use Wheeler on the final day of the regular season.
Wheeler allowed one run over six innings in a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays to help Philadelphia secure its postseason berth, but the situation left his status for the wild card round unclear.
Even though Wheeler won't get the start, Mattingly told reporters after Wednesday's 4-3 win to extend the series "it'll be pretty much all hands on deck" for Game 3.
The Phillies are fortunate to have a deep starting staff that allowed them to go with All-Stars Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez in the first two games against Atlanta.
However, Game 3 left Mattingly with a decision between Nola or Wheeler. John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia noted Wheeler has never started a game in the regular season or playoffs on short rest.
Wheeler's only relief appearance in his MLB career was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS against the Arizona Diamondbacks. He tossed 1.2 scoreless innings in a 9-7 loss.
Nola will be pitching on regular rest after starting on Saturday against the Rays. He only made it through one inning, allowing three runs on four hits in a 12-1 loss.
While Nola's overall stat line this season doesn't look great with a 4.67 ERA, he did get better as the year went on. The right-hander had a 3.33 ERA in 14 starts after the All-Star break.
Nola made three starts against Atlanta this season with two coming in a five-day span from Sept. 6-11. He allowed three runs and struck out eight over 13.1 innings in those two outings last month.
The Phillies forced Game 3 against Atlanta thanks to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hitting back-to-back homers in the eighth to tie the score at three. Alec Bohm delivered the go-ahead solo homer in the top of the 10th.
Andrew Painter finished the game on the mound with three scoreless innings out of the bullpen.
Game 3 between the Phillies and Braves from Truist Park will be played at 8 p.m. ET on Thursday. The winner will advance to play the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLDS starting on Saturday.

item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan

They wound up losing and hoped that Cristopher Sanchez could get them a Game 2 win to keep the season alive. Thanks to Sanchez, Andrew Painter, Alec Bohm, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, the Phillies won Game 2 and will play a Game 3 in a winner-takes-all matchup. But who is going to start for the Phillies? According to Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia, the Phil
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies sent Jesus Luzardo out to the mound for Game 1 of the NL Wild Card round against the Atlanta Braves. They wound up losing and hoped that Cristopher Sanchez could get them a Game 2 win to keep the season alive.
Thanks to Sanchez, Andrew Painter, Alec Bohm, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, the Phillies won Game 2 and will play a Game 3 in a winner-takes-all matchup. But who is going to start for the Phillies?
According to Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia, the Phillies have made their decision between Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola. The resurgent Nola will get the Game 3 start, as the Phillies hope to clinch Thursday night in Atlanta.
Phillies turn to Aaron Nola for Game 3 vs. Braves
"Hearing Phillies will start Aaron Nola tonight vs. Braves opener Ray Kerr, a lefty," Salisbury reports. "Always subject to change but that's the plan as of this AM."
The Phillies' plan for the winner-takes-all Game 3 of the NL Wild Card series against the Braves will be to start Nola instead of Wheeler on short rest.
While having Wheeler go would've been preferred, if there was ever a time to trust in Nola, it's this season after his second-half resurgence.
As June came to a close, his 6.04 ERA had Phillies fans, rightfully, very concerned about his massive contract going forward.
But his final 11 starts of the 2026 season resulted in an incredible 2.93 ERA. While some luck has gone his way during that stretch, his massive improvement is giving the Phillies enough confidence to turn to him for Game 3.
On the other side, the Braves are reportedly going to start Ray Kerr, a left-handed pitcher, as potentially an opener until they turn the reins over to Grant Holmes.
The Phillies have Wheeler as an option out of the bullpen for multiple innings in Game 3, but ideally they'll ride Nola for as long as possible.
If they could somehow win without pitching Wheeler, that would be the best-case scenario. The same goes for both Jesus Luzardo and Andrew Painter, both of whom would be willing to pitch in Game 3 if needed.
With how shaky the bullpen is, the Phillies are really going to need Nola to go deep into this game, unless the Phillies' offense comes alive and blows this game out of proportion, and some normal relievers can come into the game without worry of blowing it.
But the most important thing is how Nola performs, as he's expected to get the ball to start the game. It's the right call, especially considering how he's on normal rest and is more ready to go than any other pitcher on the roster.

item.title: [MLB.com] Phillies vs. Braves NL Wild Card Series Game 3 FAQ (8 ET, NBC/Peacock)
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman; Todd Zolecki; Paul Casella
item.description: In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023. “Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a lit
item.content:encoded:
In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023.
“Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a little bit, it's the same as we did [after Game 1]: Turn the page, and move on to tomorrow and show up ready to do the same thing.”
So, what could the Phillies and Braves possibly have in store for their winner-take-all showdown?
While that’s the biggest question looming over the National League Wild Card Series, it’s far from the only one. Here’s everything you need to know about Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
The game will begin at 8 p.m. ET and air on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Phillies: TBD
The Phillies planned to meet following Game 2 to discuss their pitching plans for this week’s third elimination game. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said Monday that Aaron Nola was setting up to start Game 3, but there’s no question things can change. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see ace Zack Wheeler start on short rest. If he doesn’t start, there’s no doubt he’d enter the game in relief.
Braves: TBD
Grant Holmes will attempt to handle the bulk of the innings. But the Braves haven’t said whether he’ll start or possibly follow an opener. The top options to open are left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter. Either would be tasked with handling Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber in the first inning.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: The Braves’ lineup appears much more formidable against right-handed pitchers. With Mike Yastrzemski in left field, Mauricio Dubón would move to shortstop, which was where Ha-Seong Kim started during the first two games.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Phillies: Mattingly said it’s “all hands on deck,” although closer Jhoan Duran wasn’t available in Game 2. Mattingly said he hoped he’d have Duran in Game 3. But other than Cristopher Sánchez, who started Game 2, probably every pitcher on the Phillies’ staff will be available in some capacity in Game 3. That’s everybody from Wheeler to Luzardo to Painter.
Braves: Closer Raisel Iglesias and his top setup men Didier Fuentes and Dylan Lee both pitched in the first two games of this series. Each should be available in this winner-take-all game. Robert Suarez hasn’t been utilized yet. He missed three months with an elbow ailment before making two appearances last week. But manager Walt Weiss may have no other choice but to turn to the right-hander, who posted a 0.56 ERA in 31 appearances before his elbow became a problem in June.
Any injuries of note?
Braves: OF Lane Thomas could be available during the NLDS. Starting pitchers Bryce Elder (arthroscopic knee surgery), Reynaldo López (right shoulder inflammation) and Martín Pérez (lower back discomfort) may also be available in future rounds.
Who is hot and who is not?
Phillies: Home runs often come in bunches for Schwarber and Harper. Did their back-to-back homers in the eighth inning in Game 2 get them going? Bohm is 3-for-8 with one double and one home run in the series. After struggling all season, Realmuto has two hits and two RBIs this series.
Anything else fans might want to know?
The Phillies are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.

The Phillies will try to continue their postseason dominance over the Braves in Thursday’s Game 3. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS.
In the seventh, Drake Baldwin’s double glanced off Harper’s glove in right field, driving in Sean Murphy to give Atlanta a 2-1 lead. Harper, who resumed playing the outfield late this season for the first time since 2022, got a poor jump and was leaping for the ball near the warning track. He was not charged with an error. Matt Olson added a sacrifice fly.
“Probably should have been caught, obviously,” Harper said.
The Phillies pulled even with eighth-inning home runs by Schwarber and Harper off Dylan Lee, the winning pitcher in the Braves‘ 5-3 opening win on Tuesday. Schwarber’s drive carried 447 feet and Harper followed with a 418-foot drive.
Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6 2/3 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.

The start time for the decisive Game 3 has not yet been determined. The Braves announced that MLB will schedule the game for either 2:15 p.m. ET or 8:15 p.m. ET in Atlanta, with the final time dependent on the conclusion of the other three Wild Card Series Game 2 matchups tonight.

item.title: [MLB.com] Bullpen stung by long ball after Mahle's strong playoff debut
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength. “I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength.
“I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
Nearly 40 years later, Weiss still remembers the sting he and his A’s teammates felt when an injured Gibson came off the bench to hit a walk-off homer against Hall of Fame closer Dennis Eckersley in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series at Dodger Stadium.
A similar type of sting was felt as the Braves blew a two-run eighth-inning lead in a 4-3, 10-inning loss to the Phillies in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Dylan Lee surrendered consecutive homers to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper in the eighth. Didier Fuentes allowed Alec Bohm’s decisive homer with two outs in the 10th.
“That's life,” Braves starting pitcher Tyler Mahle said. “Sometimes, it happens. There's nothing really else to say about it. It sucks now, but we're going to have a chance to go out there tomorrow and turn it around.”
Now, Weiss’ bunch must win Game 3 on Thursday to avoid being eliminated from the playoffs by Philadelphia for the fourth time overall and third time in the past five years. The Phillies eliminated Atlanta teams that won 100-plus regular-season games in 1993 (NLCS), 2022 (NLDS) and 2023 (NLDS).
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
“[The Braves] have played great at home,” Harper said. “But again, I'll just talk about the postseason; it's just a different animal.”
Mahle proved he was up to the challenge during what was his first postseason appearance. The right-hander, acquired from the Giants on Aug. 2, became the first Braves pitcher to allow one run or none over seven-plus innings in the postseason since Max Fried threw seven scoreless against the Reds in Game 1 of the 2020 NL Wild Card Series.
Once Harper misplayed a Drake Baldwin fly ball into a go-ahead double off Phillies starter Cristopher Sánchez during Atlanta’s two-run seventh, it looked like the Braves were destined for a great storyline.
But instead of celebrating how their trade acquisition helped them end the Phillies’ playoff dominance, the Braves were reminded that Lee hasn’t been nearly as good as he was before the All-Star break, when he posted a 1.47 ERA in 43 innings (44 appearances).
When Schwarber opened the eighth with a Statcast-projected 447-foot homer and Harper followed by depositing another ball into the right-field seats, Lee extended the troubles he had while posting a 6.00 ERA in 24 innings after the break. It should be noted he allowed just two homers during that stretch, and he did not allow any home runs to left-handed batters during the regular season.
“Lee’s our high-leverage lefty,” Weiss said. “He put down the same part of the order yesterday.”
Lee struck out Schwarber and got Harper to fly out in Game 1. How might he fare if he’s asked to go through these left-handed sluggers for a third straight day?
How about Fuentes? The rookie right-hander was masterful during the regular season, posting a 2.05 ERA in 70 1/3 innings as a reliever. But he surrendered J.T. Realmuto’s two-run triple in Game 1, and his psyche was bruised again Wednesday when Bohm sneaked his game-winning homer over the right-field wall.
“[Fuentes] made a good pitch,” Baldwin said. “I think if we need him tomorrow, he'll be ready to go, and I don't think he'll let that affect him too much.”
The Phillies’ rotation was a concern entering this series because Zack Wheeler was needed to pitch on Sunday with a postseason spot on the line. Well, Aaron Nola and Wheeler could be used in Game 3.
As for the Braves, they haven’t announced who will start Game 3. Grant Holmes will be lined up to pitch at least four innings. But will he start? Or will either Ray Kerr or Brent Suter take the mound as an opener?
More importantly, can the Braves bounce back from this and finally end their playoff struggles against their division rivals?
