item.content:encoded:
Inside Miz's Rise: How Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski Became MLB’s Most Unhittable Starter
This week, Brewers flamethrower and National League Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski will conclude one of the most overpowering, unhittable seasons ever recorded by a starting pitcher.
No qualified starter in modern baseball history has ever surrendered a lower opponent’s batting average than what Misiorowski is allowing now (.159). Take away the shortened 2020 season, and only one starter — Gerrit Cole in 2019 — has ever generated a higher strikeout rate over the course of a full season than Misiorowski’s 38.2% mark this year.
So, it might seem strange that MLB’s velocity king — whose triple-digit heat has reached as high as 105.5 mph, the fastest ever recorded by a starting pitcher — grew up idolizing a pitcher whose average career four-seam velocity clocked in around 90 mph.
Adam Wainwright, who can count on one hand how many big leaguers have ever told him he was one of their favorite players, was taken aback when I told him that he was Misiorowski’s childhood idol.
"He might’ve gotten the first 92, 93 mph from me," Wainwright quipped. "The other 12 are on him."
As of a month ago, Misiorowski had never met or talked to Wainwright. But as a kid in the Kansas City area with little winning baseball to watch in the early 2000s, Misiorowski was drawn to the St. Louis right-hander — not because Wainwright overwhelmed his competition with sheer force, the way Misiorowski can do, but because he was unflappable.
"The biggest thing was his demeanor on the mound," Misiorowski told me last month. "Something bad happens, move onto the next pitch. There’s no care, no emotion with it. I took that into just pitching in general. Whenever I give up a home run or something like that, ‘OK, so be it, they got to me, next pitch.’"
That, admittedly, was not always so easy for Misiorowski.
(Getty Images)
"They used to tear me up, and I’d get really upset on the mound," Misiorowski said. "Then I started watching other guys. I kind of thought about Wainwright and his demeanor and just everyone in the past and kind of was like, ‘That’s what I need to do. I need to forget about it.’"
Along with harnessing his control, adding to his powerful arsenal and maturing into his 6-foot-7-inch frame, Misiorowski’s mental growth on the mound is part of the transformation that has helped the raw prospect with elite tools develop into MLB’s most dominant starter over the course of just one year.
The best pitcher on the best team in baseball leads MLB in ERA, WHIP, strikeouts, strikeout rate and opponents’ batting average, among a litany of categories.
"Emotionally, he’s in a way better place," Brewers manager Pat Murphy told me. "I always say, your first year you’re on rollerskates. You don’t feel the concrete on the ground. It’s a little slippery. I feel like he’s taken off the rollerskates. He’s not all the way there. He’s not all the way matured. He’s going to face more adversity. But he’s handled what adversity has come his way pretty darn well."
‘Unlike Anything You Ever See’
Despite his junior college background, Misiorowski’s stuff was never a question.
The velocity that "Miz" generated from his long levers was enough to convince the Brewers to spend a second-round pick in 2022 on the gangly right-hander from Crowder College, who would otherwise have been transferring to LSU for his junior season.
(Photo by Tim Nwachukwu/Getty Images)
In his first full pro season in Milwaukee’s system in 2023, Misiorowski jumped from Low-A to High-A to Double-A, combining to strike out 110 batters in 71.1 innings. Days before Misiorowski’s first Double-A start against the Montgomery Biscuits, his pitching coach, Will Schierholz, saw him throw in person for the first time. The first pitch of the bullpen session clocked in at 98 mph. Then Misiorowski spun a slider at 92.
"We had some pretty good arms, some major league arms, on that staff, and you’re awestruck when you watch Miz throw up close for the first time," Schierholz, who’s now a Brewers assistant pitching coordinator, told me. "It’s unlike anything you ever see."
In Misiorowski’s last three starts that season, he struck out 29 batters in just 14.2 innings. He’d spike curveballs into the dirt, and opponents would still chase. He’d fire fastballs three feet above the zone, and hitters would still helplessly offer. Many times, they were simply guessing as soon as the ball left his hand.
"Every time he touched the mound, he knew hitters did not have a chance," Schierholz said. "If he made his pitch, they didn’t have a chance."
The problem, however, was that Misiorowski often didn’t know where the ball was going. In five starts at Double-A that season, Misiorowski walked 16 batters and hit 11.
"He was always ultra, ultra competitive, it just wasn’t always a consistent mindset on the mound when things maybe didn’t go his way," Schierholz recalled. "So to see kind of where that’s gone over the last couple years here, to see him have that consistent mindset, calm and collected at all times, that’s come a long way since he came up to Biloxi in 2023."
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
As the strikeouts continued to rack up a year later, so did the free passes. Over 79.2 innings at Double-A in 2024, Misiorowski struck out 105 batters, walked 50 and plunked 10.
When he was promoted to Triple-A that August, the Brewers put him in the bullpen, in part to limit his innings. He clearly had a big-league arm, but his lack of control threatened to make him a reliever long-term.
"I think that was always in the back of everybody’s head, right?" Schierholz said. "Especially for a guy with that prolific stuff. Just in general, you don’t see starters have the stuff that he has. But I think the thing that always kept all of us optimistic is the arsenal’s deep. He didn’t have a big injury history, and he was still so young that we had time to make sure this played out in a positive way."
(Photo by Olivia Vega/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Misiorowski returned to starting at the beginning of the 2025 season at Triple-A. The control issues lingered, which was part of the reason he was MLB’s No. 68 overall prospect that year and not a top-10 talent. Over a five-start stretch, he struck out 38 batters in 30.2 innings with a 0.79 ERA. But then came four starts in which he combined for 12 walks over 14 innings.
Still, despite Misiorowski’s volatility, depth issues in the Brewers’ big-league rotation spurred action. They called up the 23-year-old, who did not look overwhelmed by the promotion.
After just five MLB starts, the last of which was a six-inning, 12-strikeout gem against Clayton Kershaw and the reigning champion Dodgers, Misiorowski was named an All-Star. Some scoffed at MLB’s decision, but he looked deserving of the honor when he threw a scoreless eighth inning in an eventual National League win.
"He’s taken the game straight out of the firehose," Brewers pitching coach Chris Hook told me. "It was a lot. I thought he did an incredible job for as much as was thrown at him."
But adversity beckoned, as it does so often for rookies.
An Early Turning Point
Opponents went from hitting .138 against Misiorowski in the first half to .257 in the second half. Lefties feasted on his slider, his strikeout rate declined, his control and command remained spotty, and the Brewers wanted to be cautious of his workload, considering he had never thrown even 100 innings in a professional season.
Hook sensed Misiorowski was wearing down, both physically and mentally.
"The intensity here is higher, and then you’re pitching more often," Hook explained. "At the end of September, he felt it. It was a lot of strain."
(Photo by Olivia Vega/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
After Misiorowski registered a 5.45 ERA in nine starts out of the break, he was moved to the bullpen at the end of the season. He didn’t like the way he was handling himself or how he handled getting hit around.
So, he thought back to Wainwright. About the mindset. About letting go.
Then, he rose to the occasion with the lights at their brightest.
In a bulk relief role, Misiorowski recorded a 1.50 ERA over 12 playoff innings. His postseason ended with five innings of one-run ball at Dodger Stadium, where he struck out nine batters in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series. It wasn’t enough to lift his Brewers over the eventual back-to-back champs, but he looked at that moment as a turning point in his career.
"I went through the struggles at the end of the year, and really was trying to battle through it," Misiorowski said. "Then, postseason rolled around, had the success, and I kind of brought it into this year, still on that momentum."
He demonstrated his ability to control his emotions on baseball’s biggest stage.
Then he focused on everything else within his control — his body, his arsenal, the strike zone — to ascend into a starting pitching marvel.
"When you fail, and you’ve been one of the best pitchers on the planet and quickly one of the youngest All-Stars of all time, I’m sure that can take a toll on anybody," Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold told me. "But he’s a mature kid. He’s grown up to be a man right in front of us, and he’s a guy that you want at the front of any rotation. He’s the best pitcher in the game, in my opinion."
Controlling His Body
Over the offseason, Misiorowski went to work on building his slender frame, knowing he needed more force and stamina to hold up over the long haul of a season after last year’s dropoff.
"It was definitely more lower-body focused," he told me. "I wanted to get my legs as strong as possible. That’s where most of my power comes from."
He ended last year around 185 pounds. Crossing the 200-pound mark this winter was a milestone moment. He didn’t stop. He said he came into camp at around 215-220 pounds and is now around 210-215, a 30-pound increase from last year.
He didn’t change his diet entirely, but he acknowledged there were fewer 3 a.m. visits to Taco Bell with his friends.
"Eating well, eating better," Misiorowski explained, "not crappy, like I was. Really working on finally maturing into my body."
Where does he see the weight helping most now?
"The biggest is definitely stamina," he said. "The effort isn’t max effort every time. You can still get to the 100s, and it’s an easier effort compared to last year when I was hitting 100 and it was full go."
Of all the improvements Misiorowski has made, it’s the velocity jump that stands out most to Schierholz, his old minor-league pitching coach. What Misiorowski is doing is unmatched and unprecedented.
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
Prior to this season, the fastest average four-seamer for a qualified MLB starter over the course of a full season belonged to Noah Syndergaard at 98.9 mph in 2016. Misiorowski is averaging 100.6 mph this year, up more than a tick from a season ago.
There have been 365 occasions of a starting pitcher crossing the 102-mph mark this season. The Pirates’ Bubba Chandler did it twice. So did Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez, when he was used as an opener. The other 361 times are courtesy of Misiorowski, who has also eclipsed 103 mph 143 times, 104 mph 22 times and 105 mph once.
A year ago, he threw just 22 pitches over 102 mph, including the postseason.
"I think we try to lay out plans for the guys, but all the credit goes to him, the work that he put in," Arnold said. "You gotta want to be great, and I think Miz is exactly that kind of kid. He knew what he needed to do to get better, and he did it himself."
And now, Misiorowski has a better idea of where his four-seamer is going — even if he’s not entirely sure why.
Controlling The Zone
Misiorowski’s fastball gets the highlights and acclaim, but arguably the most dramatic and important change Misiorowski made this year has nothing to do with his power.
He has cut his walk rate down from 11% last year to 6.6% this year, the largest year-to-year drop among all qualified MLB starters.
But he can’t explain how.
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
"I honestly have no clue," Misiorowski told me. "I wish I could tell you and help everyone out. I honestly have zero idea on how I’m doing it. It’s one of those things I’m looking at like, ‘That number ain’t right.’"
Many of his teammates assumed he must be pounding the strike zone a lot more, but he’s actually in the zone less this year than he was last season.
That might seem confusing, but his pitching coach has an explanation.
"You can’t wait him out," Hook said. "He’s throwing 105 [mph], and it’s like, ‘I gotta go if he’s throwing a strike.’"
"It’s going to be hard to put the ball in play," Arnold added, "so teams are probably wanting to be aggressive and see if they can hop on something."
It helps that Misiorowski is throwing a first-pitch strike 8% more this year than last year — also the largest year-to-year jump from any qualified starter this season.
And it plays into Brewers closer Trevor Megill’s theory.
"You make one pitch a strike on the corner, then the one off the corner by three inches looks like it’s closer than it is," Megill told me.
Misiorowski’s chase rate (35.2%) is up nearly 7% from last season.
Meanwhile, his whiff rate (37.2%) is the highest among all qualified starters and is also up significantly from a year ago (29.7%) — again, that’s the biggest year-to-year jump for a starting pitcher in MLB.
Misiorowski’s enhanced ability to harness his stuff has led to shorter innings, longer outings and even a game between him and his pitching coach.
One time earlier this year, Misiorowski was coming off a 12-pitch frame when Hook issued a test.
"I said, ‘Hey, can you make it a 10 next?’ He made it a 10,’" Hook recalled. "I said, ‘Can you make it a nine?’ We just like having those challenges inside the game."
Controlling His Arsenal
Earlier this year, Cardinals shortstop Masyn Winn watched Misiorowski’s fastball up close and followed up with a question.
Why the hell are you throwing anything else?
"It was funny," Misiorowski recalled. "But on the flipside, I’m like, ‘I can’t just do that.’"
In some ways, though, Misiorowski has heeded Wynn’s advice.
His four-seam usage is up this year, and no starter in baseball throws their heater more. With a fastball that averages over 100 mph and is responsible for 163 of his MLB-leading 247 strikeouts, you can understand why.
At the same time, Misiorowski is still adding to his repertoire.
"It seems to me like he went home and said, ‘You know what, the postseason was fun, I want to get back there again, how can I be a great pitcher and not just a thrower?’" Wainwright said. "That is the nature of how great players mature. That’s the nature of how great players grow in the game. They don’t get comfortable in who they are. They don’t get stuck."
Last year, lefties hit .385 and righties hit .267 against Misiorowski’s slider, which averaged 5 mph slower than his four-seamer. The Brewers wanted to find another offering that would create more of a separation in velocity.
So, Misiorowski added a slower slider with more depth to his arsenal this year, which righties are hitting .188 against. Meanwhile, he turned last year’s slider into his cutter, which lefties are hitting .089 against this season.
"I’ve gotten a lot of strange looks, strange emotions, from it, just in the fact that the cutter’s kind of closer to the heater," Misiorowski said. "You get some swings where some guys see the spin, and then they’re like, ‘Oh, shoot, it’s on me.’"
(Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
In addition to his curveball and changeup, the new additions to his arsenal give opponents more to think about this season beyond his velocity.
"He kind of does things on the fly a little bit," Hook said. "I’m not saying he’s a lab kid, per se. He’s naturally gifted, and he’s like, ‘I’m going to do this,’ ‘I can do that,’ and he makes the adjustment."
Along with a lower walk rate, Misiorowski’s strikeout rate is up 6.2% from last season and is the highest in MLB. He won’t win the triple crown — Phillies ace Cristopher Sánchez has three more wins than him — but he leads the sport in both ERA and strikeouts, despite ranking 23rd in innings pitched.
His triple-digit heat combined with better control and command certainly help, but so does the tweak in his repertoire. He’s also gaining a better feel for game-planning and why his catchers are calling for certain pitches in certain situations.
"At the start of the year, we were definitely more, ‘Whatever you think, let’s just roll with it. You’re obviously seeing something that’s working,’" Misiorowski told me. "And it’s gotten to the point where it’s like, ‘OK, I’m kinda seeing it too. I understand where you’re going with this."
‘This Guy Is Built For This’
More often than not, though, he relies on his catchers to help him navigate a game, as William Contreras did during his 15-strikeout, one-hit, complete-game shutout on 95 pitches against the Phillies in June.
Contreras also helped Misiorowski work around trouble two months later, when the pitcher made his return to the mound at Dodger Stadium for the first time since the NLCS.
(Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images)
A year ago, Misiorowski was stupefied watching Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman sign his jersey at the All-Star Game. In some ways, he’s still that wide-eyed kid, pinching himself about his new reality.
"I don’t think that will ever get to a point where it’s just normal," Misiorowski told me.
Only now, he’s starting to gain the poise of the idols he grew up watching.
The day before his start on Aug. 15, Misiorowski’s newfound confidence was on full display when he gave away his attack plan against Ohtani.
"He knows what I’m going to do: I’m going to throw a heater," Misiorowski vowed. "Good luck. Here it is."
Sure enough, he followed up on those words by attacking Ohtani with six straight fastballs in his first at-bat, all over 102 mph, to induce a popout. But it’s what Misiorowski did in his final at-bat against Ohtani that exemplified why he is so much more than the novice flamethrower he was a year ago.
After three straight singles off Misiorowski in the fifth inning, Ohtani stepped to the plate with the bases loaded and one out. This time, at Contreras’ behest, Misiorowski switched it up. He got a swinging strike on a curveball, a called strike on a four-seamer, then sent Ohtani back to the dugout swinging through a slider.
"He’s thinking more like a pitcher," Contreras told me, "and not just wanting to throw hard."
(Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images)
One batter later, Misiorowski used the slider again to fool Freddie Freeman on a strikeout and escape the threat. He pumped his fist and let out a scream before returning to the dugout.
As he attempts to follow Wainwright’s lead with his composure on the mound, he’s not losing himself in the process.
"That part of his game hasn’t changed, which I’m happy to see," Schierholz said. "That’s part of what makes him special, is the competitiveness and pitching with emotion, as long as he continues to rein it in and keep it in control."
The Brewers are counting on that as they rumble toward the best record in baseball for a second straight season, this time hoping their Cy Young favorite can help them author a new ending to their franchise’s winningest chapter.
"Obviously, it’s a different animal when you get into October," Misiorowski said. "But it’s going to be exciting, and I think we have a team that can make a run at it."
"This guy," Hook added, "is built for this."

item.description: BOSTON (AP) — Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia's Cristopher Sánchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single, and the Boston Red Sox edged Cleveland 1-0 on Wednesday night to snap the Guardians' six-game winning streak. item.content:encoded:
BOSTON (AP) — Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia's Cristopher Sánchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single, and the Boston Red Sox edged Cleveland 1-0 on Wednesday night to snap the Guardians' six-game winning streak.
It was just the fifth win in 13 games for the Red Sox, who clinched a playoff spot on Sunday.
The 36-year-old Gray (18-5) is in line to become the fourth Red Sox pitcher since 2000 to lead the AL in victories, joining Rick Porcello (2016), Josh Beckett ('07) and Curt Schilling ('04).
Gray allowed four singles, struck out three, walked one and lowered his ERA to 2.72.
Aroldis Chapman struck out the side in the ninth for his 35th save of the season.
Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) gave up a run on 10 hits with seven strikeouts.
The Guardians entered with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the AL Central after winning the series opener Tuesday, but needed a win Wednesday combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros to clinch a postseason berth.
The victory came with a price for the Red Sox when center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela left with right hamstring tightness after running out a single the same day he was activated from the injured list. He had been sidelined with a right a quad strain since Sept. 3 and made a diving headlong grab on Steven Kwan, the game's first batter.

item.title: [tsn.ca] Blue Jays finish season sitting 16th in MLB Power Rankings
item.dc:creator: ESPN

item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

item.title: [bleacherreport.com] Yordan Alvarez, Jacob Misiorowski, AL, NL Stat Leaders Ahead of 2026 MLB Season's Final Weekend
item.dc:creator: Adam Wells
item.description: Yordan Alvarez, Jacob Misiorowski, AL, NL Stat Leaders Ahead of 2026 MLB Season's Final Weekend With five days remaining in the 2026 MLB regular season, the individual stats leaderboard is almost as unsettled as the playoff races in both leagues. The key races going into the final weekend involve Yordan Alvarez's quest for the AL triple crown and Jacob Misiorowski looking to lead all of MLB in strikeouts. Here are the leaders in several individual categories going into Wednesday's games. TOP NEW
item.content:encoded:
Yordan Alvarez, Jacob Misiorowski, AL, NL Stat Leaders Ahead of 2026 MLB Season's Final Weekend
With five days remaining in the 2026 MLB regular season, the individual stats leaderboard is almost as unsettled as the playoff races in both leagues.
The key races going into the final weekend involve Yordan Alvarez's quest for the AL triple crown and Jacob Misiorowski looking to lead all of MLB in strikeouts.
Here are the leaders in several individual categories going into Wednesday's games.
TOP NEWS
Teams Scouting Cespedes' Son 🤯
Ranking MLB's 10 Greatest Postseason Runs Since 2000 🏆
Rays' Revamped Throwback Uni 🔥
| Category | American League | National League |
| Batting Average | Yordan Alvarez (Astros): .314 | Luis Arraez (Phillies): .314 |
| Home Runs | Alvarez (Astros) and Junior Caminero (Rays): 41 | Kyle Schwarber (Phillies) and Pete Crow-Armstrong (Cubs): 45 |
| RBI | Pete Alonso (Orioles): 108 | Alec Burleson (Cardinals): 111 |
| Hits | Yandy Diaz (Rays): 175 | Otto Lopez (Marlins): 186 |
| Stolen Bases | Chandler Simpson (Rays): 46 | Nasim Nunez (Nationals): 47 |
| Wins | Sonny Gray (Red Sox): 17 | Cristopher Sánchez (Phillies): 18 |
| Innings | Michael Wacha (Royals): 194.1 | Sandy Alcantara (Marlins): 212.0 |
| ERA | Cam Schlittler (Yankees): 1.94 | Jacob Misiorowski (Brewers): 1.86 |
| Strikeouts | Gavin Williams (Guardians): 244 | Jacob Misiorowski (Brewers): 247 |
| Saves | Bryan Baker (Rays) and Cade Smith (Guardians): 40 | Riley O'Brien (Cardinals): 38 |
Alvarez will need a strong close to the season to win the triple crown. He still leads the AL in average and is tied for the lead in homers, but his RBI pace has fallen off this month.
The Houston Astros star had just five RBI in his first 16 games in September before driving in three on Tuesday in a 7-0 win over the Seattle Mariners.
Alvarez is up to 102 RBI for the season. Pete Alonso's 17 RBI this month have pushed him up to 108 with five games remaining.
Alvarez and Luis Arraez are tied for the MLB lead with a .314 batting average. Both players look like safe bets to maintain that position through Sunday.
Misiorowski, the biggest breakout star of the season for the 2026 NL Central champion Milwaukee Brewers, is looking to become the first pitcher to lead MLB in both ERA and strikeouts in a 162-game season since Jake Peavy in 2007.
The MLB ERA title is down to Misiorowski at 1.86 and New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler at 1.94. Misiorowski will likely get one more abbreviated start in Milwaukee's final regular-season series against the St. Louis Cardinals.
Schlittler is scheduled to make his final regular-season start on Thursday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Since the Yankees are locked into the No. 4 seed, he is also likely to have a shortened outing to prepare for Game 1 of the wild-card round on Tuesday.
The strikeout race is arguably more compelling than the ERA title because Gavin Williams of the Cleveland Guardians will likely get the nod on Friday against the Kansas City Royals.
Since the Guardians can't wrap up the AL Central until Friday at the earliest, Williams will likely have a regular outing. He is currently only three Ks behind Misiorowski for the MLB lead.
Williams has 15 strikeouts in 11.2 innings against the Royals this season, but he hasn't faced them since May 5.
NL MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong is one stolen base away from the seventh player in MLB history to have a 40-40 season. He can also become the first Chicago Cubs player to lead the NL in homers since Sammy Sosa hit 49 in 2002.

item.content:encoded:
In what will likely be his last regular season start for the Atlanta Braves this season, Chris Sale will be facing off against Andrew Abbott and the Cincinnati Reds.
Chris Sale is not the front runner for the Cy Young award, but will most certainly get some second and third place votes with his 2.18 ERA, 30.3 percent strikeout rate, and league leading strikeout to walk ratio of 6.13. Sale also leads the NL is best HR rate of 0.5 per nine innings, and best walk rate in the NL of 4.9 percent.
Side note, Chris Sale has the best career strikeout to walk ratio of all-time. Sale has also pitched 157.0 innings thus far this season, which is hurting his Cy Young chances to guys like Jacob Misiorowski. It could be argued that he has passed his fellow competitor Cristopher Sánchez, but Sánchez has a whopping 200.0 IP which is second in MLB behind Sandy Alcantara.
The Braves got a scare yesterday when Ronald Acuña fouled a ball off his shin, but luckily all the tests came back negative. The Braves have already clinched the division so a loss to the Reds yesterday was not a huge deal except the chances of a playoff bye are quickly fading. The offense looked bad again, so hopefully they can catch a spark again before the playoffs take off.
No Braves player has faced Abbott more than five at-bats. Ha-Seong Kim has a HR in his four at-bats and Ozzie Albies has a .600 average. Michael Harris has struggled to an OPS of .400 in his five at-bats, and Mauricio Dubón and Mike Yastrzemski are hitless in their three at-bats. Austin Riley is also hitless in five at-bats.
It is hard to make any type of prediction on such a limited history, but we can look at Abbott's numbers and see his 4.70 ERA is approximately eleven percent below average and his 1.472 WHIP is the worst of his four year career. This season he has struggled with walks giving up 4.2 per nine innings. The Braves need to be patient this even and take advantage of his weakness. It is no secret that the Braves struggle in the walk department. Their 7.7 percent is the third worst in MLB. To be fair, they strike out at a lower rate than the average team this season, but walks get runners on base to knock in.
The Reds are in the bottom six in RP ERA this season. The Braves have feasted on RPs all season long. The key to the game tonight seems to be be patient against Abbott because he gives up a lot of walks. Get to the bullpen, and strike. Chris Sale should keep the runs low to make this a pretty easy win on paper. The question is how many players will be resting today, especially with a high likelihood that Acuña will be letting his leg heal.
First pitch is at 7:15 EDT.
Game Info
Game Time: Wednesday, September 23rd, 7:15 pm EDT
Location: Truist Park, Atlanta, GA
Watch: BravesVision
Radio/Audio: 680 AM / 93.7 FM The Fan

item.title: [thebiglead.com] Don Mattingly offers Jesús Luzardo update ahead of Phillies postseason

item.content:encoded:
As the 2026 MLB season concludes, the Philadelphia Phillies are days away from clinching a postseason berth for the fifth straight year. The club is currently 86-70 and the No. 6 seed in the National League.
Philadelphia is four games up on the outside-looking-in Arizona Diamondbacks, and only one game back of both the San Diego Padres and Chicago Cubs for the higher Wild Card seeds.
The Phillies, if they make the playoffs, will have to play in the best-of-three Wild Card round. One would have to think that lefty ace Cristopher Sánchez and veteran righty Zack Wheeler will pitch.
That being said, their best pitcher over the last few months has been presently injured left-hander Jesús Luzardo. Before landing on the 15-day injured list with left shoulder inflammation retroactive to Sept. 12, he had a 1.65 ERA with 124 strikeouts in his 14 most recent starts.
Luzardo’s playoff availability
An injury like pitching arm shoulder inflammation can be tricky when it comes to putting a timeline on it. Luzardo apparently suffered the injury after his Labor Day start versus the Atlanta Braves, so he has been out of action for approximately two weeks.
The Wild Card round runs from Sept. 29 through Oct. 1, so it may be doubtful that Luzardo can make a start for that series. However, it may be possible for him to take on a bullpen role.
When asked on Tuesday, Phillies manager Don Mattingly said that Luzardo is “trending in the right direction.” The quote was reported by Tim Kelly of OnPattison.
Phillies’ postseason outlook
If the season ended today, the Phillies would take on their division rival Braves in Atlanta for the Wild Card round. If they take that series, they would then play the Los Angeles Dodgers at their house.
If Luzardo is not a go for the Wild Card, then the club will perhaps need to find a capable Game 3 starter. That would likely put longtime Phillie Aaron Nola on the bump. Though his season numbers are not great, he has pitched exceptionally well lately.
Nola’s run as of late included back-to-back starts against the Braves early in September, where he twirled 13 ⅓ innings while allowing only three runs. He could be a worthy option if Luzardo cannot go.

item.title: [MLB.com] Wheeler llega a los 2,000 ponches en su carrera para guiar triunfo de Filis
item.dc:creator: Todd Zolecki
item.description: El martes por la noche, continuó dejando huella en el partido contra los Cerveceros en el Citizens Bank Park. No solo ponchó a los tres bateadores de la primera entrada, sino que también ponchó a Brice Turang para registrar el número 2,000 de su carrera. Zack Wheeler estableció un récord para los Filis al ponchar a los primeros siete bateadores del encuentro en una victoria por 6-4 sobre los Cerveceros (98-59), superando la marca de Brandon Duckworth de seis ponches seguidos para comenzar un par
item.content:encoded:
El martes por la noche, continuó dejando huella en el partido contra los Cerveceros en el Citizens Bank Park. No solo ponchó a los tres bateadores de la primera entrada, sino que también ponchó a Brice Turang para registrar el número 2,000 de su carrera.
Zack Wheeler estableció un récord para los Filis al ponchar a los primeros siete bateadores del encuentro en una victoria por 6-4 sobre los Cerveceros (98-59), superando la marca de Brandon Duckworth de seis ponches seguidos para comenzar un partido el 5 de agosto del 2002 contra los Dodgers. El ponche de Wheeler en el primer episodio ante Brice Turang fue el número 2,000 de su carrera.
Wheeler es el 96to lanzador en la historia de MLB en alcanzar los 2,000 ponches. Su compañero de equipo, Aaron Nola, llegó a esa misma cifra a principios de esta temporada. Son la segunda pareja de compañeros de equipo que alcanza dicha marca en una misma temporada, los primeros en lograrlo fueron Tim Hudson y Jake Peavy con los Gigantes en 2014.
El lanzador derecho de 36 años fue más allá al ponchar a siete bateadores consecutivos al inicio del juego, superando así el récord anterior de la franquicia de seis ponches, establecido por Brandon Duckworth en 2002.
Fue una salida fantástica contra el mejor equipo en todo el béisbol, un club al que Filadelfia podría enfrentar en la SDLN. Los Filis anotaron tres carreras en la octava entrada contra el bullpen de los Cerveceros para llevarse el triunfo.
Pero Milwaukee fabricó una carrera en el cuarto capítulo para reducir la ventaja de los Filis a 3-1. Sin embargo, en el sexto inning, un sencillo al iniciar la entrada, un boleto con un out, un doble robo y un sencillo con dos outs del venezolano William Contreras anotaron dos carreras para empatar el partido.
Jake Bauers le siguió con otro sencillo con dos outs. Fue el 101er pitcheo de la jornada para Wheeler.
Mattingly dijo antes del juego que esperaba mantener a Wheeler en cerca de 90 lanzamientos, teniendo en cuenta que podría ser su última apertura de la campaña regular. Ahora, el próximo turno de Wheeler en la rotación es el último compromiso de la temporada regular el domingo contra los Rays, pero si los Filis aseguran el Comodín de la Liga Nacional antes del domingo, podría abrir el Juego 1 de la Serie de Comodines el martes.
Los Filis quieren a Wheeler lo más fresco posible, porque si pretenden ganar esa serie al mejor de tres, casi con certeza será debido a un excelente pitcheo abridor por parte de Wheeler, el dominicano Cristopher Sánchez y otros.
La escuadra de Filadelfia (87-70) terminó el choque con la esperanza de que los Diamondbacks (82-74) cayeran ante los Rockies la noche del martes. Ganando o perdiendo, los Filis todavía podrían asegurar un quinto viaje consecutivo a la postemporada tan pronto como el miércoles.

item.title: [phillyvoice.com] The Phillies aren't serious
item.dc:creator: Nick Tricome PhillyVoice Staff
item.description: September 22, 2026 The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back. But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go. item.content:encoded:
September 22, 2026
The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back.
But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go.
Brooks Raley loaded the bases in relief of Andrew Painter one out into the bottom of the sixth, and with a one-run lead, then gave up a Brett Baty liner into center that a diving Justin Crawford could only trap between his glove and the grass for another Mets run scored – and with the bases still full.
Interim manager Don Mattingly yanked Raley as soon as he could for Chase Shugart, and he walked in another to Ronny Mauricio – a .173 hitter at the bottom of the New York order – before a warning-track flyout from Francisco Lindor mercifully ended the frame.
The Phillies set themselves up with a bases-loaded answer of their own in the top of the seventh, after Trea Turner and Alec Bohm drew walks and Luis Arráez singled around a Kyle Schwarber groundout and a Bryce Harper strikeout. But under the pressure situation, Bryson Stott hacked a roller through the grass to second and was left slamming his helmet into the dirt as the Mets jogged back to their dugout without any damage.
The night unraveled from there. The Phillies lost to the Mets, 10-3, up in Queens. Orion Kerkering got tagged for the second straight game, letting up four more runs in the eighth, then was demoted to Triple-A after in a move that essentially exiles the struggling reliever from the roster.
They came back with a 7-2 win the next day, behind a stellar outing from ace Cristopher Sánchez that salvaged a 2-2 split in a four-game series, but with the whole weekend taken into account, it wasn't any kind of silver lining.
The Phillies are supposed to be a playoff team, and still more than likely will be, but they had four games against a Mets club living in the NL East basement right there for the taking. It was the schedule's last gimme. And yet they couldn't help but throw two of those games down the gutter, for little other reason than that they couldn't get out of their own way.
The Phillies were supposed to, or at least wanted fans to think, that they turned over a new leaf at the plate, hitting through August with the kind of small ball approach that their power-heavy lineup went out of its way to avoid for way too long, but they've since reverted back to the old habits and stubborn cold streaks that have long overstayed their welcome.
And the Phillies were supposed to have, or rather praying for, a somewhat stable bullpen after the trade deadline, but now it's so fickle and with so little time left that decisions seem destined to come down to "what starter moves into the bullpen for the postseason?"
It's been this way for five years now, through many big-money contracts that feel like they're never quite living up to the price tag, through many more failed looks at bargain-bin arms, two (and what's looking on track to be three) managerial changes, a dramatic infield shuffle mid-season, and increasingly suspect prospect development that begs an increasingly scarier question of what kind of long-term future does this club really have?
The Phillies aren't a serious baseball team. Not anymore, at least.
They're still good, sure, in the sense that they can – and again, more than likely will – qualify for a spot in October.
But really, they could've locked that spot up a week ago.
Instead, they're 8-10 through September. They punted any possible shot at the NL East title out the window once they let the Braves go 4-3 against them across their final two series, and left a Diamondbacks club that has notoriously broken their hearts before with a faint (and therefore dangerous) glimmer of hope in the final NL Wild Card chase, while leaving a best-of-three road playoff series in Atlanta as the expected prize.
And oh yeah, they do still have to play two good teams that can easily exhaust and bury them before the Phils can even think about any of what might come after.
So where really is the contender in all of this?
Certainly the Phillies are going to lean on their elite starters between Sánchez, Zack Wheeler, a revitalized Aaron Nola, and Jesús Luzardo if they can get him back in time, but at the same time, that wasn't enough against the Mets in the 2024 NLDS or the Dodgers in the 2025 division series a year later. They each countered with shutdown pitching on their side, and hung in there until the Phillies inevitably had to reach into their volatile bullpen to capitalize.
And nothing about the 2026 club suggests that this time would be any different; not when Braves and Dodgers can continue to match them beat for beat talent-wise, while having already proved that they both play much smarter games – in the field, at the plate, and even more so on the base paths – and definitely not after they just showed that they're apparently not that much further above the lowly Mets.
Brandon Marsh, who had an All-Star first half, has one extra-base hit this month.
J.T. Realmuto, once labeled the best catcher in baseball, struck out six times in the Mets series and is a .213 hitter in his mid-30s.
Luis Arráez, who has batted well above .300 for years, suddenly dipped to a .285 average as a Phillie, and while Alec Bohm is impressing with a .328 average through the month, he's never going to hit with the power many hoped for out of a former first-round draft pick at a listed 6'4" and isn't going to suddenly discover it now at age 30 while heading toward free agency.
That leaves Harper and Schwarber as the star sluggers, but at this point, as bats who can be managed around or even directly challenged, while Turner seems to perpetually volley between a $300 million force one minute and a guy who looks like he forgot how to play shortstop the next.
Here's the catch, too: the above names are either in their late 20s at their youngest or pushing well into their 30s on average, after repeated years of trying and failing to out-thump the competition, and with not many more shots expected to be left, especially now that a labor strike puts a serious threat over 2027.
The Phils had a great August, but that was always with a tough September schedule looming, which was always going to tell you what kind of team they really were.
And while there are still six games left, and a probable postseason clinch, there's enough of a picture to tell you this: The Phillies aren't serious.
They haven't been, and really, unless something way more drastic happened at the deadline or Crawford or Painter instantly became the new faces of the franchise, that reality was staring everyone in the face all winter – when the only noticeable difference to the lineup was that Nick Castellanos wasn't in it anymore.
Are they still good enough for October? To get there, sure...probably...hopefully, after this week?
But any further than that? No. They haven't shown anything to say otherwise, or that they're any different from the last two Phillies clubs that hit a hard stop.
Follow Nick on Twitter: @itssnick
Follow Nick on Bluesky: @itssnick
Like us on Facebook: PhillyVoice Sports
