item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, the Philadelphia Phillies will open up a series with the Milwaukee Brewers (at home).
They had the day off on Monday following a four-game series with the New York Mets at Citi Field.
The Phillies split four games with the Mets (and most recently won by a score of 7-2 on Sunday).
Cristopher Sanchez got the start.
He allowed just two earned runs in 6.1 innings.
Phillies Star Cristopher Sanchez Sends Out 13-Word Post
Ahead of Tuesday’s series with the Brewers, Sanchez sent out a post to Instagram.
He wrote: “Different stadiums, different uniforms, same focus and the same plan: contribute to winning 🔥❤️”
There were over 10,000 likes on his post in less than 24 hours.
Looking At Sanchez
Sanchez is in the middle of his 6th season at the MLB level (all with the Phillies).
He is a two-time MLB All-Star.
Right now, the 29-year-old is 18-6 with a 2.93 ERA in 32 starts.
Looking At The Phillies Right Now
The Phillies are the second-place team in the National League East with an 86-70 record in 156 games.
They have gone 4-6 over their last ten games (and are 41-34 in 75 games at home).
Following the Brewers, the Phillies will play their final series of the 2026 regular season when they host the Tampa Bay Rays.
Scott Lauber of The Philadelphia Inquirer wrote (on Monday): “Brewers-Phillies pitching matchups: Tuesday- RHP Dustin May (7-9, 4.61) vs. RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 2.99) Wednesday- RHP Logan Henderson (10-3, 2.51) vs. RHP Aaron Nola (7-10, 4.49) Thursday- TBD vs. TBD”
Looking At The Brewers Right Now
The Brewers are the top team in the National League Central with a 98-58 record in 156 games.
They have gone 8-2 over their last ten games (and are 46-32 in 78 games on the road).
Following the Phillies, the Brewers will finish the regular season (at home) when they host the St. Louis Cardinals.

item.title: [The Ringer] Baseball’s Best Pitchers Aren’t Worth What They Used to Be (But Its Best Batters Are)
item.description: On Sunday, as MLB’s regular season reached its one-week warning, the two most spectacular players of 2026 strutted their stuff. In Cincinnati, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong singled, doubled, and hit his 45th home run in a 9-1 trouncing of the Reds. (He also stole his 38th base, putting him on the precipice of joining the 40-40 club.) Hours later, at Camden Yards, Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski held the Orioles to one hit and lowered his ERA to 1.86 as the Brewers blanked Baltimore 3-0 f
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, as MLB’s regular season reached its one-week warning, the two most spectacular players of 2026 strutted their stuff. In Cincinnati, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong singled, doubled, and hit his 45th home run in a 9-1 trouncing of the Reds. (He also stole his 38th base, putting him on the precipice of joining the 40-40 club.) Hours later, at Camden Yards, Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski held the Orioles to one hit and lowered his ERA to 1.86 as the Brewers blanked Baltimore 3-0 for their major-league-leading (and franchise-record) 98th win.
A season’s most sensational player isn’t always its most valuable player—see Cal Raleigh last year—but PCA and the Miz check both boxes. They lead the majors in FanGraphs WAR for hitters and pitchers, respectively, and will win the MVP and Cy Young awards in the National League (which has established itself as the stronger circuit by owning the American League 375–323 in interleague play). PCA and the Miz; the Miz and PCA: Already All-Stars in 2025, they’ve made large leaps this year. The Cub has bolstered his bat speed and drawn more walks; the Brewer has upped his pitch speed and issued fewer walks. Born nine days apart in the spring of 2002, the two 24-year-old terrors of the NL Central have set the standards for hitting and pitching excellence and, in the process, made themselves the player stories of the season. In an MLB campaign whose compressed standings have caused fans to wonder which teams, if any, are actually good (especially in the AL, where the .500 Rangers lead the AL West), the left-handed hitter and right-handed hurler—whose clubs may meet in October—have left little doubt about their own extreme skills.
There’s also little doubt about how those skills stack up against each other—or, at least, what those skills are worth when they’re applied on the field. The “WAR leader” label lumps PCA and Misiorowski together as peerless players. If we had to choose between them, though, the answer would be easy: The Miz wins most of their head-to-head battles, but PCA wins the WAR. Crow-Armstrong, who’s hit .280/.371/.578 with superlative defense in center, has been much more valuable than Misiorowski, who’s held hitters to a .159/.225/.250 line and who’s struck out 247 batters (including PCA six times) while walking only 42 (including PCA twice). That’s no surprise: It’s now the norm for baseball’s best hitter to be a good deal better, WAR-wise, than baseball’s best pitcher. Which, in turn, tells us a lot about how hitter and pitcher usage—and entertainment value—have evolved.
Take Sunday’s action. PCA played the whole game in center, even though the Cubs had built a comfortable lead by the halfway point. The Miz, meanwhile, exited after three innings and 44 pitches, with the Brew Crew clinging to a 1-0 lead. With home field advantage throughout October up for grabs, Milwaukee still had something to play for. But the Brewers elected to take it easy on their flamethrower, who has already exceeded his 2025 workload (including the playoffs) by 28 innings. As a result, Misiorowski amassed just 62 percent of the WAR PCA did on Sunday—and, on the whole, he’s managed only 63 percent of the WAR PCA has produced this season (6.5 vs. 10.4).
It wasn’t always the case that baseball’s best hitter would leave baseball’s best pitcher in his dust on the combined WAR leaderboard. The chart below compares the values of FanGraphs’ hitting and pitching WAR leaders for each season dating back to the beginning of the DH era in 1973. To smooth out year-to-year variation, each bar represents a five-year rolling average of the annual hitter-minus-pitcher WAR gaps from the listed season plus the four preceding seasons. Thus, the value for 1973 is really the average of the figures from 1969 to 1973, and the value for 2026 is really the average of the figures from 2022 to 2026.
At the dawn of the DH era, when the iron men of the mound were still routinely topping 300 innings, the best pitchers were worth more than the best hitters. Pitchers also reigned supreme around the turn of the century, when the likes of Roger Clemens, Kevin Brown, and Randy Johnson were still topping 250 dominant innings, and Pedro Martínez posted the best pitching season ever by fWAR in 1999 (in a then-paltry 213 1/3 innings, which would lead both leagues in 2026). All in all, from the beginning of the DH era through the end of the 20th century, the leading hitter in any given year was worth only about half a WAR more than the leading pitcher, on average. From 1970 through 2000, the best hitter out-WARed the best pitcher 18 times, while a pitcher took the top spot 13 times. The battle for the title of baseball’s best player was typically close to a toss-up between the most overpowering pitcher and the biggest bat.
Over the past quarter century, though, the hitters have won in a walk. Beginning with 2001, when Barry Bonds morphed into his BALCO-boosted final form, the leading hitter has been about two wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher, enough to declare a conclusive victor despite the metric’s margin of error. During that span, best hitters have led best pitchers 25 seasons to one, with only Corbin Burnes’s slim edge over Trea Turner in 2021 preventing a clean sweep. And the gap is growing: Over the past five years, the leading hitter has been a full four wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher. In other words, baseball’s best pitchers aren’t worth what they used to be—but its best batters are.
This isn’t just a function of the no. 1 hitter lapping the no. 1 pitcher; although the average leads are less pronounced, the same trend appears when we expand the pool to each year’s top five hitters and top five pitchers.
The wide disparity in recent seasons stems in part from an unusually strong run by baseball’s best hitters. The average of 10.4 WAR generated by the hitting WAR leaders in the past five years (Aaron Judge three times, and Ronald Acuña Jr. and PCA once each) is the highest total of any five-season stretch since Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, and Albert Pujols in the early-to-mid 2000s—and, before that, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, and Ernie Banks in the late 1950s and Babe Ruth, Jimmie Foxx, and Lou Gehrig in the early 1930s. But it’s also a product of the lowest-ever five-year average WAR tally for pitching pacers (6.4), with the exception of the pandemic-suppressed 2019 to 2023 period and a late-’50s stretch of historically lackluster leading arms.
The culprit isn’t much of a mystery: It’s the playing-time totals. Modern pitchers are working smarter, not harder. (Or, if we want to be charitable, similarly hard, but in shorter bursts.) Collectively, pitchers throw roughly the same number of innings as ever, and accrue just as much WAR. (FanGraphs allots 1,000 WAR leaguewide per season, with 57 percent going to hitters and 43 percent apportioned to pitchers.) But those innings and WAR are distributed across many more arms than they used to be, as innings eating nears extinction and the starting-pitcher protagonist of the past fades from view. This season will either match last year’s all-time full-season low of three 200-plus-inning pitchers, or further reduce the record, depending on whether Michael Wacha (who’s sitting at 194 1/3 frames) joins Sandy Alcantara and Cristopher Sánchez in the 200-inning club in his final start.
Modern major leaguers’ workload diminution is much more apparent for pitchers than hitters. The chart below shows the number of hitters and pitchers who qualified for the batting title and ERA title, respectively, in each season of MLB’s 30-team era (since 1998, excluding 2020). The height of the bars (blue for hitters, orange for pitchers) indicates the number of qualifying players; the numbers above each bar (which could still increase slightly for 2026) denote the average number of plate appearances or innings within each year’s qualifying cohort.
Matt Olson aside, hitters aren’t totally immune to load management. Relative to the late 1990s, the number of qualifying hitters per season has sunk by about 15 percent, and the average number of plate appearances among qualifying hitters has been trimmed by a couple percent. But that’s nothing compared to the cratering of pitcher playing time. The number of qualifying pitchers per season has plummeted by nearly 50 percent, and the average number of innings among the remaining qualifiers has dropped by upwards of 10 percent.
Hence the ho-hum WAR totals mustered of late by baseball’s best pitchers, in an era of familiarity-effect avoidance, rampant pitcher injuries and, relatedly, an increased emphasis on max-effort throwing. As dazzling as today’s top arms are on an inning-per-inning basis—especially fastball-slider monsters like Mason Miller, whose outings are mostly contained to one frame—their GIFable filth comes at a cost. They can’t have both blistering stuff and exceptional staying power.
There’s no perfect substitute for the bulk starters used to supply. In 2019, for instance, Astros starter Gerrit Cole broke J.R. Richard’s single-season franchise record for strikeouts, 40 years after Richard’s nasty 1979 campaign. That accomplishment led to a sentimental meeting on the mound between past and present Astros aces, less than two years before Richard’s death. But although Cole surpassed Richard’s strikeout total, he couldn’t match his complete contribution: Richard threw 80 more innings, and recorded 8.9 WAR to Cole’s 7.5. Even Cole’s 212 1/3 innings in 2019 would be a standout total today; beyond Burnes in 2021, no pitcher since Cole has broken the 7-WAR wall.
On a long enough timescale, almost everything in sports circles back around. Someday, new rules might restore the starter’s lost luster, or overdue expansion might lower the major league replacement level and make the most competent pitchers look like WARlords again. League-leading hitters of the 2020s may be mogging their pitching counterparts when we focus on the DH era, but if we go back to the beginning of the National League, when hurlers who threw 400, 500, or 600 innings ruled the roost, we spot two subsequent stretches when the best bats had it even better than they do now: that late-’50s, offense-friendly low ebb for aces, and the 1920s and early ’30s, when Babe Ruth reinvented offense and broke baseball’s value scale. Once upon a time (or two), this batter-pitcher imbalance wasn’t so strange.
For now, though, we seem to be stuck in a phase where the cream of the crop of pitchers pales in comparison to elite everyday dudes. The sinking ceiling of starting-pitcher value may have implications for how pitchers are paid and staffs are assembled (not to mention how prospects are hyped). Free-agent pitchers make as much money per win as free-agent hitters, but if teams start expecting fewer wins from star pitchers than they do from star hitters, even the scarcity of healthy ligaments might not keep pitcher contracts from shrinking (and dragging down overall player pay). From the fan perspective, though, the more relevant byproduct of this modern mismatch in the value of leading hitters and pitchers is a shift in how we experience and describe standout seasons.
Because hitter playing-time totals today are comparable to what they were a century ago, we can still celebrate league-leading hitters via counting stats alone. PCA, for example, has played in every Cubs game this season, and started all but one. (As of today, he’s the majors’ sole 700-plate-appearance man.) We can convey his greatness just by marveling at how many homers he’s hit and bases he’s swiped; “the first 40-40 center fielder” would sound spiffy. If we want to dig deeper, we could note that only Triple Crown contender Yordan Alvarez stands in the way of PCA becoming the first player ever to lead the majors in both batting and fielding value in a single season, which would be a two-way feat almost as mind-blowing as Shohei Ohtani’s pitching/hitting heroics. And if we want to cite WAR, well, that’s easy: With six Cubs games to go, PCA’s season already ranks among the 50 best batting years in big league history, and above every season in the past half century save for four by Bonds, two by Judge, and one by Bobby Witt Jr.
In 2026, pitchers tend not to throw enough pitches or innings to reach famous milestones in single games, single seasons, or careers, so the case for Miz amazement can’t be made by hailing his membership in exclusive, storied clubs. With one regular-season start remaining, the Miz hasn’t quite cracked the top 350 seasons by pitching WAR. (No pitcher has posted a double-digit-WAR season since the Big Unit in 2001.) The 300-strikeout club has been closed to new recruits since Cole and his teammate Justin Verlander went in together in 2019. As for old-school wins, he’s tied for second in the Senior Circuit with 15, not that anyone pays much attention to that column on the player page.
To appreciate the Miz, we must resort to rate stats and modest minimums. Among pitchers with at least 160 innings in a season, Misiorowski ranks 13th in park- and league-adjusted ERA, 12th in park- and league-adjusted FIP, third in WHIP and strikeout-minus-walk rate, and second in strikeout rate. He has the lowest opponent batting average and rate of hits allowed per nine innings, too, which would be more eye-popping if people still cared about batting average or if the league were hitting more than .244. Ultimately, the summation rests on the smallest of samples: a single pitch. At peak pitch speed, he’s the hardest-throwing starter on record (and in all likelihood, ever), and damn near the hardest-throwing pitcher, period.
In a sense, the Miz is just as impactful as PCA—he just hasn’t had as many chances to make an impact. PCA has paired his 702 trips to the plate (offensive chances, essentially) with 380 chances in center, for a grand total of 1,082 opportunities to determine the outcome of a plate appearance. Misiorowski has faced 646 batters, or 60 percent of PCA’s combined plate appearances plus defensive chances. If we look at things that way—i.e., by doing dubious addition—then the Miz has done well to accumulate 63 percent of PCA’s WAR.
Plus, in defense of Misiorowski and the constellation of starters who trail him by 1 WAR or less—AL Cy Young lock Cam Schlittler, Cristopher Sánchez, Chris Sale, Jesús Luzardo, and Dylan Cease—the tale of the 2026 WAR leader is as much about Crow-Armstrong vs. the field as it is pitchers vs. hitters. Only Ohtani and Witt sit between PCA and Misiorowski on FanGraphs’ WAR leaderboard, and both only barely lead the Miz. WAR is always subject to retroactive updates, but if none of the players clustered between 6.4 and 6.7 WAR—Ohtani, Misiorowski, Witt, and Alvarez—finishes strong, this could be the first unabridged season since 1950 (when teams played 154 games) in which MLB’s second-most-valuable player doesn’t touch 7 WAR. Fittingly, the AL’s MVP contenders are as underwhelming as the AL’s contending teams.
“Underwhelming” doesn’t describe Misiorowski. Of course, the quality that makes the Miz so awe-inspiring—he throws hard enough to remove a mortal’s arm from its socket—is also what makes him so anxiety-inducing. It’s not as if hitters can’t get hurt by running, throwing, or swinging hard—or even by standing somewhere in the vicinity of the on-deck circle, as Crow-Armstrong’s teammate Alex Bregman (whose WAR total since the All-Star break is exceeded only by PCA’s) painfully learned on Sunday. But they aren’t as prone to season-ending disaster as a matter of routine.
We delight in PCA’s uninhibited, prolific play, while we watch the Miz’s impressive but sparing appearances through splayed fingers. As Joe Posnanski pointed out in July, pitching might be the only assignment in sports where “simply doing your job is so scary and treacherous.” Not because an opposing player might flatten you, or because you might, say, stumble and get sliced by a skate blade, but because the fundamental motion endemic to your duty is hazardous to your health. Which helps explain why teams have sought to limit how often pitchers perform that motion, for all the good it’s done them. As it turns out, making that motion more dangerous but doing it less doesn’t make UCLs safer.
Misiorowski has survived the season with only minor, sporadic complaints: a hamstring cramp here, a dead arm there. To forestall more serious trouble, and to preserve their most prized pitcher for the postseason, the Brewers have handled him carefully. Since the All-Star Game (which he missed), he’s tied for 72nd in innings pitched, with two pitchers (Jack Perkins and Zebby Matthews) who have matching 4.94 ERAs over that span. But in October, when off days allow for compression of a pitching staff, an unrestrained Miz may emerge to shoulder more of Milwaukee’s workload and make overmatched opponents and concerned spectators alike quake like Ralph Wiggum. Over a season, or even a series, a position player such as PCA may amass more value. But in any given game, an ace can still slay.

item.title: [MLB.com] Claros favoritos en la última encuesta del JMV, pero ¿podrá esta semana cambiar algo?
item.dc:creator: Brian Murphy
item.description: Mientras marchamos por la última semana de la temporada regular, no parece haber mucho suspenso respecto a quiénes serán nombrados JMV. Al menos, eso es lo que podemos descifrar de nuestra más reciente -- y última -- encuesta del JMV de MLB.com para el 2026. El cubano Yordan Álvarez sigue estando bien al frente en la Liga Americana a pesar de una producción relativamente mediocre recientemente. En la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong está cerrando una de las mejores campañas completas en tiempo
item.content:encoded:
Mientras marchamos por la última semana de la temporada regular, no parece haber mucho suspenso respecto a quiénes serán nombrados JMV. Al menos, eso es lo que podemos descifrar de nuestra más reciente -- y última -- encuesta del JMV de MLB.com para el 2026.
El cubano Yordan Álvarez sigue estando bien al frente en la Liga Americana a pesar de una producción relativamente mediocre recientemente. En la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong está cerrando una de las mejores campañas completas en tiempos recientes.
Treinta y ocho expertos de MLB.com emitieron sus votos sobre quiénes creen que se llevarán los honores de JMV tras esta temporada, con 32 jugadores recibiendo al menos un voto. Como recordatorio, los votos se basaron no solo en el desempeño hasta ahora, sino también en cómo se espera que evolucionen las cosas durante el resto de la campaña.
Los votantes clasificaron a sus cinco principales candidatos de cada liga con un sistema de 5-4-3-2-1: cinco puntos por un voto al primer lugar, cuatro por el segundo, y así sucesivamente. Estos son los resultados.
Todas las estadísticas son hasta la jornada del domingo, a menos que se indique lo contrario.
LIGA AMERICANA
Álvarez ha tenido un desempeño tan bueno este año que lo que califica como un bache para él sería un gran trecho para la mayoría de los demás bateadores. En sus últimos 41 encuentros, batea .264 con OPS de .840. Reiteramos, nada mal para la mayoría, pero muy por debajo del nivel del líder de la Americana en promedio (.313) y OPS (1.027). Álvarez lleva tres cuadrangulares y cinco impulsadas a lo largo de 16 partidos este mes, dejándolo a un jonrón del dominicano Junior Caminero de los Rays por el liderato en el Joven Circuito y a seis empujadas de Pete Alonso por la cima en dicho departamento. Aunque sus posibilidades de la Triple Corona se están desvaneciendo un poco, Álvarez todavía ha armado un 2026 asombroso en el plato. Su wRC+ de 179 es al menos 27 puntos mejor que el de cualquier otro bateador calificado.
Sabemos que el quisqueyano es uno de los grandes cañoneros del juego. Está cerrando su segunda temporada consecutiva de 40 vuelacercas y está dando swings más fuerte que nadie. Pero lo que ha sido más impresionante de su temporada es su mejorado criterio en la zona de strike. Aumentó su tasa de boletos desde un 6.3% por debajo del promedio a un 11.5%, lo que se ubica en el 80mo percentil de MLB. También ha mantenido una tasa de ponches muy sólida (18.5%). Ya no persigue tantos pitcheos fuera de la zona, ha reducido su tasa de swings en blanco y está haciendo más contacto en general. Esa mezcla de paciencia, trueno y control del bate es una combinación especial, sobre todo en un jugador de 23 años. Luciendo un porcentaje de embasarse de .363 (52 puntos mejor que la campaña pasada), el OPS de .892 de Caminero se ubica tercero en la Americana.
Witt ha tenido mejores campañas a la ofensiva, aunque 18 bambinazos, 43 estafadas y wRC+ de 119 en 137 partidos no está nada mal. Pero cuando se consideran todas sus capacidades, Witt sigue siendo extremadamente valioso. Su valor de carreras defensivas de +16 está empatado en el tercer lugar de las Grandes Ligas, y sus 22 outs por encima del promedio encabezan la Liga Americana. También cuenta con un valor de carreras en el corrido de bases de +8, a uno de Corbin Carroll de los Diamondbacks por el liderato de MLB. Por eso, aunque no ha sido tan indiscutible en la caja de bateo como lo fue en el 2024 (wRC+ de 169), la grandeza integral de Witt lo tiene en la cima de la tabla de posiciones de WAR de FanGraphs en el Joven Circuito (6.6) y posiblemente perfilándolo entre los primeros cinco en la votación para JMV por tercera vez en tres años.
Ha habido bastante conversación de JMV entorno a Schlittler en las últimas semanas. ¿Y por qué no? Está marcando el paso en la Americana en efectividad (1.94), WHIP (0.91) y WAR de pitcheo de FanGraphs (6.1). Se ubica segundo en el Joven Circuito en promedio de bateo en contra (.182) y en tasa de ponches menos boletos (25.0%). Ha permitido una carrera o ninguna en 21 aperturas. Ese es un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees y algo que apenas otros dos lanzadores de 25 años o menos han logrado en la Era de la Pelota Viva (desde 1920): Blake Snell (2018) y Dean Chance (1964). Seguramente será reconocido con el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana a estas alturas, pero Schlittler recibirá su merecida cuota de consideración para el JMV.
Schlittler no ha sido el único miembro de los Bombarderos que ha sido indispensable este año. Mientras Nueva York ha estado sin Aaron Judge durante una gran parte de la campaña y ha echado de menos a otros bates estelares debido a lesiones, Rice ha sido demostrado consistencia. Se ubica tercero en el Joven Circuito en jonrones (39) y anotadas (100). Es cuarto en la liga en impulsadas (95) y OPS (.888), y está empatado en el cuarto lugar en valor de carreras al bate (+34). Con dos vuelacercas durante la última semana, Rice se convertiría en apenas el segundo miembro del equipo del Bronx diferente a Judge en la última década en conectar al menos 41 jonrones en una temporada, acompañando al dominicano Juan Soto (2024).
Otros que recibieron votos: El venezolano Willson Contreras, Medias Rojas; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigres; el cubano Miguel Vargas, Medias Blancas; el cubano Randy Arozarena, Marineros; Munetaka Murakami, Medias Blancas; Dylan Cease, Azulejos.
LIGA NACIONAL
El mes pasado, PCA dio el salto por encima de Ohtani hacia el puesto Nro. 1 de nuestra encuesta. Este mes, se ha apartado por completo del resto del grupo. Crow-Armstrong, quien recibió cada voto de primer lugar emitido por nuestro panel, está empatado con Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de bambinazos de MLB (45). Nadie tiene más anotadas (118), extrabases (83) o total de bases anotadas (351) esta campaña. Con 38 estafadas, el dinámico jardinero central del equipo del Norte de Chicago podría convertirse en el séptimo miembro del club 40-40 más adelante esta semana. Y no pase por alto el hecho de que es posiblemente el mejor jugador a la defensa en cualquier posición en estos momentos. Ya no es una cuestión de si Crow-Armstrong es el JMV de la Nacional. El premio es prácticamente suyo ahora mismo. Pero ¿lo ganará de manera unánime?
Ohtani se mantiene como el claro escolta en el Viejo Circuito a pesar de haber jugado en apenas tres partidos este mes debido a sus persistentes lesiones en la rodilla izquierda y el bíceps derecho. La buena noticia es que el dirigente de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, dijo que "hay una buena posibilidad" de que Ohtani sea activado de la lista de lesionados de 15 días el miércoles tras cumplir la estadía mínima. No lanzará por el resto de la temporada, dejándolo con efectividad de 1.79 y 95 ponches en 85.2 entradas. Pero Ohtani tendrá unos cuantos partidos para sumar a sus totales ofensivos (30 jonrones, wRC+ de 142).
Mencionamos antes cómo Schlittler luce como el gran favorito para el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Misiorowski tendría su premio más asegurado en la Nacional. A lo largo de 169.1 episodios, Miz encabeza la Gran Carpa en casi cada categoría, incluyendo efectividad (1.86), WHIP (0.80), tasa de ponches menos boletos (31.7%) y fWAR (6.5), por nombrar solo algunas. Sus oponentes tienen un diminuto OPS de .474 contra Misiorowski, la segunda menor cifra para cualquier abridor calificado en la Era Divisional (desde 1969). Los oponentes del quisqueyano Pedro Martínez, en una de las mejores campañas para un lanzador, registraron OPS de .473 en el 2000.
El dominicano, quien no recibió un solo voto en nuestra anterior encuesta de JMV, ha estado encendido con Cincinnati durante el último mes. En sus últimos 27 encuentros, batea .404 con ocho vuelacercas, seis bases robadas y OPS de 1.205. Dio múltiples hits en 14 de esos partidos, y su fWAR de 2.5 durante este transcurso es el mejor de las Mayores. Esta prolongada racha encendida le ha dado a De la Cruz un wRC+ de 139 -- el mejor de su carrera -- y lo deja a dos jonrones más dos estafadas de convertirse en el cuarto jugador de los Rojos en el club 30-30 y el primero desde Brandon Phillips en el 2007.
Schwarber ha caído en un pequeño bache, bateando de 34-4 con un cuadrangular en sus últimos 10 encuentros. También está a ocho ponches de establecer un récord de ponches en una misma campaña. De todas maneras, hay que admirar la consistencia de Schwarber. Terminará con más de 40 vuelacercas y 150 juegos disputados en cuatro de las últimas cinco temporadas. Ha superado los 100 boletos negociados por cuarto año consecutivo, y un tercer título de bambinazos del Viejo Circuito está a su alcance.
Otros que recibieron votos: El dominicano Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Cerveceros; Matt Olson, Bravos; James Wood, Nacionales; Jordan Walker, Cardenales; Alex Bregman, Cachorros; Bryce Harper, Filis; Jake Bauers, Cerveceros; el dominicano Otto López, Marlins; el venezolano Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Rafael Devers, Gigantes; Alec Burleson, Cardenales; CJ Abrams, Nacionales; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Cristopher Sánchez, Filis.

item.title: [MLB.com] Our final MVP poll has clear frontrunners, but can this week change anything?
item.dc:creator: Brian Murphy
item.description: As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll. Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory. Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they
item.content:encoded:
As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll.
Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory.
Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they think will earn MVP honors after this season, with 32 players receiving at least one vote. As a reminder, votes were based not only on results so far, but also on how things are expected to play out the rest of the season.
Voters ranked their top five picks in each league on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on. Here are the results.
All stats are through Sunday unless otherwise noted.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Alvarez has been so good this year that what qualifies as a slump for him would be a good stretch for most other hitters. Over his past 41 games, he is hitting .264 with an .840 OPS. Again, not bad for most, but well below the standard of the AL leader in average (.313) and OPS (1.027). Alvarez has three homers and five RBIs through 16 games this month, leaving him tied with the O's Pete Alonso and one home run behind the Rays' Junior Caminero for the AL lead and nine RBIs behind Alonso for the top spot in that statistic. Even though his Triple Crown chances have faded, Alvarez has still put together an awesome 2026 at the plate. His 179 wRC+ is at least 27 points better than any other qualified hitter.
We know Caminero is one of the game's great sluggers. He is finishing up his second straight 40-homer season and swings harder than anyone. But what's been most impressive about his season is his improved strike-zone judgment. He has upped his walk rate from a below-average 6.3% to 11.5%, which ranks in the 80th percentile of MLB. He's also maintained a very solid strikeout rate (18.5%). He's not chasing as much, has shaved his whiff rate and is making more contact overall. That blend of patience, power and bat control is a special combination, especially in a 23-year-old player. Carrying a .363 on-base percentage (52 points better than last season), Caminero's .892 OPS ranks third in the AL.
Witt has had better offensive seasons, although 18 homers, 43 steals and a 119 wRC+ in 137 games is not too shabby. But when you consider his entire skill set, Witt remains extremely valuable. His +16 fielding run value is tied for third in the Majors, and his 22 outs above average tops the AL. He also has a +8 baserunning run value, one behind the D-backs' Corbin Carroll for the MLB lead. So while he hasn't been as undeniable in the batter's box as he was in 2024 (169 wRC+), Witt's all-around greatness has him atop the AL FanGraphs WAR leaderboard (6.6) and in line for a possible top-five finish in the MVP voting for the third time in three years.
There has been quite a bit of MVP chatter surrounding Schlittler in recent weeks. And why not? He is pacing the AL in ERA (1.94), WHIP (0.91) and FanGraphs pitching WAR (6.1). He ranks second in the junior circuit in opponents' batting average (.182) and strikeout-minus-walk rate (25.0%). He has allowed one or zero runs in 21 starts. That's a Yankees franchise record and something only two other pitchers age-25 or younger have accomplished in the Live Ball Era (since 1920): Blake Snell (2018) and Dean Chance (1964). He seems like a lock for the AL Cy Young Award at this point, but Schlittler will receive his fair share of MVP love.
Schlittler hasn't been the only indispensable Yankee this year. While New York has been without Aaron Judge for a large portion of the season and has missed other star bats as well due to injuries, Rice has been a constant. He ranks third in the AL in homers (39) and runs scored (100). He's fourth in the league in RBIs (95) and OPS (.888), and tied for fourth in batting run value (+34). With two homers during the final week, Rice would become just the second non-Judge Yankee over the past decade to hit at least 41 homers in a season, joining Juan Soto (2024).
Others receiving votes: Willson Contreras, Red Sox; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigers; Miguel Vargas, White Sox; Randy Arozarena, Mariners; Munetaka Murakami, White Sox; Dylan Cease, Blue Jays
NATIONAL LEAGUE
Last month, PCA jumped over Ohtani and into the No. 1 spot in our poll. This month, he has run away from the rest of the field. The recipient of every first-place vote cast by our panel, Crow-Armstrong is tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs (45). No one has more runs (118), extra-base hits (83) or total bases (351) this season. With 38 steals, the Cubs' dynamic center fielder could become the seventh member of the 40-40 club later this week. Oh, and let's not overlook the fact that he is arguably the best defensive player at any position right now. It's no longer a question of whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP. The award is as good as his right now. But will he win it in unanimous fashion?
Ohtani remains the clear runner-up in the NL despite playing in just three games this month due to his nagging left knee and right biceps injuries. The good news is Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said "there's a good chance" Ohtani will be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday after a minimum stint. He won't pitch for the rest of the season, leaving him with a 1.79 ERA and 95 K's over 85 2/3 innings. But Ohtani will have a few games to add to his offensive totals (30 homers, 142 wRC+).
We mentioned earlier how Schlittler looks like the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young Award. Misiorowski is an even bigger shoo-in in the senior circuit. Through 169 1/3 innings, Miz leads the Majors in just about every category, including ERA (1.86), WHIP (0.80), strikeout-minus-walk rate (31.7%) and fWAR (6.5), to name just a few. Opposing batters have a scant .474 OPS against Misiorowski, which is the second-lowest by any qualified starter in the Divisional Era (since 1969). Pedro Martinez, in one of the greatest seasons by a pitcher, recorded a .473 opponents' OPS in 2000.
De La Cruz, who didn't receive a single vote in our previous MVP poll, has been red-hot for Cincinnati over the past month. In his last 27 games, he is batting .404 with eight homers, six steals and a 1.205 OPS. He collected multiple hits in 14 of those games, and his 2.5 fWAR during this period is the best in the big leagues. This prolonged hot streak has given De La Cruz a career-best 139 wRC+ and has left him two homers and two steals away from becoming the fourth Red in the 30-30 club and the first since Brandon Phillips in 2007.
Schwarber has fallen into a bit of a rut, going 4-for-34 with one home run over his past 10 games. He's also eight strikeouts away from setting a new record for K's in a single season. Even so, you have to admire Schwarber's consistency. He will end up with more than 40 homers and 150 games played in four of the past five seasons. He has surpassed 100 walks for a fourth consecutive season, and a third NL home run title is right there for the taking, too.
Others receiving votes: Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Brewers; Matt Olson, Braves; James Wood, Nationals; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Alex Bregman, Cubs; Bryce Harper, Phillies; Jake Bauers, Brewers; Otto Lopez, Marlins; Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; Rafael Devers, Giants; Alec Burleson, Cardinals; CJ Abrams, Nationals; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies

item.title: [inquirer.com] What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
item.dc:creator: Lochlahn March
item.description: What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more With their magic number down to three, a fifth straight postseason is in sight for the Phillies. But there are plenty of questions going into the final homestand of the regular season. The Phillies returned from their final road trip of the season with work to do. Their magic number to clinch a postseason berth is three. Any combination of wins and Diamondbacks losses that totals three wi
item.content:encoded:
What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
With their magic number down to three, a fifth straight postseason is in sight for the Phillies. But there are plenty of questions going into the final homestand of the regular season.
The Phillies returned from their final road trip of the season with work to do.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason berth is three. Any combination of wins and Diamondbacks losses that totals three will ensure the Phillies’ season continues beyond Sunday. But while they remain in control of their own destiny, it won’t be easy.
To close out the final week, the Phillies host the top team in the National League in the Brewers, followed by the top team in the American League in the Rays.
Here are a few takeaways heading into the last homestand of the regular season:
Multi-inning McFarlane
The circle of trust in the Phillies bullpen right now is extremely small. The relief unit has a 5.50 ERA in September, and the club took the drastic measure of optioning Orion Kerkering to triple-A Lehigh Valley on Sunday after his struggles became untenable. Unless there is an injury to another member of the staff, he is ineligible to be on the wild-card roster.
While the Phillies’ rotation and closer Jhoan Duran are among the best in the sport, it’s the bridge between them that has been the biggest issue. The Phillies continue to hope Jonathan Bowlan (groin) will be available for the postseason. The right-hander began playing catch Sunday, and reported to the field on Monday’s off day to continue his progress.
Before the injury, Bowlan had been going through a rough stretch, having allowed a run in five of his last six appearances. Even if he were a full go, it would be hard to imagine tossing him right back into an eighth-inning, high-leverage role after spending some time on the shelf.
» READ MORE: Phillies send struggling reliever Orion Kerkering to triple A
Enter Alex McFarlane.
The 25-year-old rookie came through in a big spot against the Mets on Sunday, facing two tough opponents in Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto to get out of a seventh-inning jam. By retiring both of them, McFarlane added a few more notches to his belt, which already included such stars as Shohei Ohtani, Mike Trout, and Nolan Arenado.
But Sunday’s win over the Mets also revealed how interim manager Don Mattingly is planning to handle his relievers in the postseason. After McFarlane struck out Soto to preserve a two-run lead with his 18th pitch, there was initially no movement in the Phillies’ bullpen during the eighth. When the Phillies loaded the bases, that’s when Chase Shugart started getting ready.
Had the Phillies’ lead stayed at two, though, Mattingly was going to send McFarlane back out. Duran would have then started warming to relieve him, and then finish it off in the ninth.
It didn’t wind up happening, but Mattingly envisions using McFarlane and Duran to cover the last nine outs of a close game.
“I think it is [realistic] this time of year,” Mattingly said. “I mean, I think with Jho, you also get to the point where he’s capable of two innings. You’re just trying to get the guys that we need in the game, for as much as you can.”
So while the lack of relief depth is still a concern, things will operate a bit differently in the playoffs. The trusted high-leverage arms, as few as they are, can and will be called upon to do more.
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly thinks Chase Shugart can take on a bigger role in Phillies' bullpen
McFarlane has thrown more than one inning just once in the two months he’s been in the majors, covering 1⅓ innings Aug. 15 against the Twins. He said he is ready to do whatever he’s asked.
“Just grateful for the opportunity,” McFarlane said. “Whatever opportunity he gives me, I’m just gonna take it one game at a time. Make sure I prepare my best, and just give all I can anytime he sends me out there.”
Starters in relief
The Phillies still haven’t mapped out how they will deploy their rotation in a wild-card series. That’s because there are a lot of unknowns: whether they will make it at all, who they will play if they do, and the health of Jesús Luzardo.
The club is “very optimistic” about Luzardo’s progress from the shoulder inflammation that landed him on the injured list, according to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. Like Bowlan, he has also progressed to playing catch.
Should Luzardo remain on track to return in time for the postseason, Dombrowski said the Phillies are keeping their options open with how they deploy him. It could be as a starter, which might be a risk given his last outing will have been Sept. 7. It could also be as a reliever, a role Luzardo has less experience in, but experience nonetheless. In the deciding Game 4 of the 2025 National League Division Series, he held off the Dodgers for 1⅔ innings of emergency relief in extras, pitching on short rest.
» READ MORE: The Zack Wheeler conversation: Why he ‘expected’ to thrive after surgery, and how much longer he wants to play
His performance in that role was largely overshadowed by how the game ended, with Kerkering botching a bases-loaded grounder to allow Los Angeles to walk it off. Had Kerkering made the throw to end the inning and things turned out differently, Luzardo’s clutch bullpen appearance might have gone down as legendary instead.
Whether or not Luzardo is one of them, the Phillies bullpen will be getting reinforcements by way of the rotation for the postseason. The question is who.
“Some of our starters are going to end up in the bullpen,” Dombrowski said. “I don’t know how it’s going to work at this point, but some of them will, especially when you get to the first round. We’re going to be the best-of-three, so you only can start three guys at that point. So you got two other guys that can go into the bullpen.”
It’s difficult to see a world where Zack Wheeler or Cristopher Sánchez aren’t starting two of the wild-card games. Aaron Nola has continued his second-half resurgence with a 2.15 ERA since Aug. 3, but he has never been a reliever in any capacity during his major league career, regular season or postseason.
Rookie Andrew Painter continues to be under consideration for making the move. He gave up four runs in his last start against the Mets, but the quality of his stuff remained high. Painter’s first inning especially stood out, when he got Lindor to ground out before striking out Soto and Bo Bichette.
Painter touched 99.4 mph with his fastball in the fifth inning. In a shorter stint, it isn’t hard to imagine him getting into the triple digits.
“I think his stuff will be very solid out there,” Dombrowski said.
» READ MORE: Andrew Painter’s potential role on a Phillies playoff staff is uncertain. Painter says any role is OK with him.
If the opportunity arises in the final six games, Mattingly said he could see the Phillies test-driving that theory by trying Painter out in the bullpen ahead of the playoffs. That said, time is running out.
Painter doesn’t think he necessarily needs a trial run to feel comfortable pitching in relief, however. He has experience with his routine shifting already, pitching behind an opener earlier this year and also appearing in relief after being scratched from his start because of a migraine.
“I feel like postseason baseball, in that atmosphere, the adrenaline is going to be flowing,” Painter said. “I don’t really think there’s much of an adjustment that’s going to be there. I think the adrenaline would just take over from that point.”
More patience from Turner
Whether the Phillies’ offense will get hot at the right time or slide back into a familiar October slumber remains to be seen. But there were some positive signs, particularly from the top of their order, in the series against the Mets.
En route to the series split, it was the top half of the order that carried a lot of the load — excluding a key bases-loaded triple from nine-hole hitter Justin Crawford on Sunday. And that’s how it will need to be for the Phillies to make a deep run.
They didn’t do it with the long ball, as the Phillies’ only two home runs in the series came from Derek Hill and Edmundo Sosa. Instead, they got on base, moved runners, and strung together hits.
Trea Turner in particular had a strong series. He finished 4-for-13 (.308), but the real eye-popping stat was his .526 on-base percentage.
» READ MORE: Can Trea Turner rescue his season despite career-worst stats at the plate? His manager and teammates believe so.
If he could maintain some of that momentum, it would be transformative for the Phillies. What has been a disappointing season by most measures for Turner could be rescued with a strong postseason performance.
“I think more and more, you see how they’re pitching him, and it’s I think basically not throwing him strikes,” Mattingly said of Turner.
According to StatCast, 53.6% of the pitches Turner has seen this year are out of the strike zone. It’s a few percentage points higher than the 51.3% out-of-zone pitches he saw last year, and trails only Kyle Schwarber (54.8%) and Bryce Harper (57.4%) among Turner’s teammates.
The difference has been that Turner swings at those out-of-zone pitches at a much higher clip. His chase rate this year is 34.6%, the second-highest of his career.
But against the Mets, he showed a glimpse of what he could be if he homes in on his selectivity. Turner drew six walks in the four-game series. He also scored three runs.
“The more he walks, the more they’re forced in the strike zone,” Mattingly said. “And when he’s on base, obviously it creates a danger there with him running and things like that. We need him to get on base. When he’s on base, we’re better.”

item.title: [fansided.com] MLB Power Rankings: Playoff stakes rise as October contenders make their move
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers; Mark Powell
item.description: The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series. item.content:encoded:
The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.title: [cbssports.com] Why Paul Skenes blames the World Baseball Classic for decreased velocity as Pirates ace wraps up down season
item.dc:creator: Mike Axisa
item.description: Despite an active offseason and a busy trade deadline, the Pittsburgh Pirates were officially eliminated from postseason contention this past weekend. At 79-77, they have a chance to finish with a winning record for the first time since 2018, but that is the smallest of consolations. The Pirates made moves intending to contend this year, but missed the postseason. item.content:encoded:
Despite an active offseason and a busy trade deadline, the Pittsburgh Pirates were officially eliminated from postseason contention this past weekend. At 79-77, they have a chance to finish with a winning record for the first time since 2018, but that is the smallest of consolations. The Pirates made moves intending to contend this year, but missed the postseason.
One reason -- maybe the biggest reason, but not the only reason -- that the Pirates missed the postseason is a down year by reigning Cy Young winner Paul Skenes. A down year that included some outright bad stretches. Skenes has a 3.91 ERA in 168 innings this season, but from May 17 to July 31, he had a 14-start stretch with a 5.18 ERA. Pittsburgh went 3-11 in those 14 games.
Over the weekend, Skenes acknowledged that the World Baseball Classic may have contributed to his fluctuating velocity and down year because it interrupted his usual spring training buildup.
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don't want to put everything on that, but I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit," Skenes told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. "Usually that time of year, you're kind of ramping up and it's a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body. One live (batting practice), you're topping at 97, and then the next you're 98, 99. And that wasn't the case this year. Looking back, I don't think that really helped."
Skenes made two starts for Team USA in the WBC, which has strict pitch limits and rest requirements, and allowed one run in 8 ⅓ innings. He did not make it out of the first inning on Opening Day, in part because his defense betrayed him, then Skenes put together a dominant eight-start stretch in which he pitched to a 1.09 ERA and averaged over six innings per start.
The rough stretch began after that, as did the velocity decline. And to be clear, Skenes still threw very hard. There were just more 95s and 96s and fewer 98s and 99s. Overall, Skenes averaged 96.8 mph with his fastball this year, down from 98.2 mph last year and 98.9 mph the year before that. He did not throw a single 100 mph pitch for the first time in his three MLB seasons.
"I didn't really have a number on it, but I would have liked to throw harder than I have this year," Skenes told the Post-Gazette. "Unfortunately, it's probably going to take an offseason to get (the velocity) back. Yeah, it's just tough."
The single most important thing is health and there's no chance -- zero -- the Pirates would have allowed Skenes to continue taking the ball every fifth day if there was a known injury. More than anything, his mechanics seemed out of whack, and mechanical fixes aren't always quick and easy, especially in-season. How much the WBC contributed to that, we don't know, but Skenes believes it was a factor.
Several other pitchers who participated in the WBC have had down years, including Skenes' USA teammate Logan Webb, but there's also a long list of pitchers who have thrived after the WBC. Nolan McLean, Eduardo Rodriguez, Cristopher Sánchez, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are among them. They played in the WBC and have been among baseball's best pitchers in 2026.
Skenes, 24, is 14th among all pitchers in WAR despite his down season. He is looking at a record payday for a pitcher in his first year of arbitration eligibility this offseason. Skenes will become a free agent after the 2029 season.

item.title: [Currently.com] Phillies’ Zack Wheeler Embraces Final Starts, ‘Winding Down’ Ahead Of Retirement
item.dc:creator: Peter Chawaga; Contributor
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies are entering the final weeks of the regular season with their margin for error narrowing. Their bullpen has remained a major concern, putting even more pressure on a starting rotation that has already dealt with injuries and inconsistency as October approaches. Until emerging star Jesus Luzardo can return from the injured list, questions about the bridge between the team's rotation and elite closer Jhoan Duran will continue to grow. The Phillies continue to rely on ques
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies are entering the final weeks of the regular season with their margin for error narrowing. Their bullpen has remained a major concern, putting even more pressure on a starting rotation that has already dealt with injuries and inconsistency as October approaches.
Until emerging star Jesus Luzardo can return from the injured list, questions about the bridge between the team's rotation and elite closer Jhoan Duran will continue to grow. The Phillies continue to rely on questionable bridge relievers, like Alex McFarlane, Jonathan Bowlan and Tim Mayza.
"Until then, the bridge from Zack Wheeler and Cristopher Sanchez to Duran is murkier than ever," Matt Gelb wrote for The Athletic. "McFarlane, a veteran of 15 big-league games, is vital to everything. So is Bowlan's health. Mayza has gained importance. So has Chase Shugart, used mostly as a long reliever all season."
Among the starts, that uncertainty makes Wheeler's role particularly important as the veteran right-hander approaches a crossroads in his career.
Philadelphia Phillies Superstar Zack Wheeler Reflects On Final Remaining Starts
Amid an impressive return from surgery and with only one year remaining on his contract, Wheeler acknowledged that he is nearing the end of his playing days.
Wheeler is pitching at a high level again after a blood clot near his right shoulder led to surgery for venous thoracic outlet syndrome, forcing him to miss the remainder of that season.
He returned in April and has since reestablished himself as arguably the Phillies' most important rotation anchor. On September 16, Wheeler threw seven scoreless innings against the Washington Nationals, allowing four hits and one walk while striking out five. The performance lowered his ERA to 2.99 through 26 starts.
But even while competing at that level, Wheeler has begun looking at some of his remaining road trips differently. During a trip this season to the Boston Red Sox's Fenway Park, for instance, Wheeler drank in the historic surroundings as he acknowledged he could be preparing for his final start in that ballpark.
"Part of that's me probably winding down my career," Wheeler explained, according to The Philadelphia Inquirer's Scott Lauber. "I've only got one more year on this contract. I don't know if I'm going to play after that. But just going into those stadiums that maybe I won't go back to — Anaheim, Detroit, Boston — we're not going to play those teams there next year. So, kind of just soaking that in and enjoying it a little bit more this year than most years."
Philadelphia Phillies Relying On Zack Wheeler As Career Nears End
The timing of Wheeler's comments is notable for a Phillies team that needs its starting pitchers to carry an increasingly heavy load.
Wheeler's recent rebound has provided some stability. He followed a difficult stretch in August with four consecutive starts of at least six innings while allowing one run or fewer, including his seven-inning shutout of Washington.
Now, the Phillies need that version of Wheeler to continue into October.
For Wheeler, however, the remaining starts also carry a personal significance. Whether his current contract represents the final chapter remains undecided, but he has clearly begun appreciating the possibility that some of these ballparks and moments could be among his last.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

item.title: [purplerow.com] Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
item.dc:creator: James Riggenbach
item.description: The Colorado Rockies are 57–99. Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take? One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball. These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out. The team with
item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.content:encoded:
Cristopher Sánchez consigue su 18ma victoria, líder de MLB; Juan Soto se va de 4-1
El dominicano Cristopher Sánchez consiguió su 18.ª victoria, la mayor cantidad en las Grandes Ligas, para guiar la victoria el domingo 7-2 de los Filis de Filadelfia ante los Mets de Nueva York.
Los Filis (86-70), que rescataron un empate en la serie de cuatro juegos, llegaron al domingo en el tercer puesto de comodín de la Liga Nacional, a un juego de los Cachorros de Chicago y Padres de San Diego y con una ventaja de cuatro juegos sobre los Diamondbacks de Arizona.
Sánchez permitió seis hits —incluido el jonrón de Bo Bichette en la sexta entrada— y ponchó a seis en 6 1/3 innings, con lo que rompió el empate con Sonny Gray, de los Medias Rojas de Boston, por el liderato de victorias en las Grandes Ligas.
El último lanzador de los Filis en liderar las mayores en victorias fue Steve Carlton, con 23 en 1982.
Justin Crawford conectó un triple de tres carreras y el venezolano Luis Arráez terminó con dos carreras impulsadas. Alec Bohm y Trea Turner aportaron cada uno un hit productor. Kyle Schwarber igualó su máximo de carrera con cuatro bases por bolas.
El novato Jonah Tong (2-2) permitió cuatro carreras y ponchó a cinco en 4 2/3 innings por los coleros Mets, que terminaron 36-45 en casa —su peor registro en Citi Field desde 2013, que fue de 33-48.
Los Mets atrajeron a 2.712.120 aficionados esta temporada, una caída de 5.870 aficionados por juego respecto a la temporada pasada —el descenso más pronunciado en las Grandes Ligas.
El dominicano Juan Soto bateó de 4-1.
